papers.title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation
papers.summary: Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) fits an amortized conditional density estimator to a simulated training set of complete-data realizations. NPE's training objective, log-likelihood, favors posterior approximations that assign arbitrarily high density to the training points, and typical families of amortized conditional density estimators (e.g., normalizing flows, Gaussian encoders) are flexible enough to oblige. The resulting policy of extreme overconfidence translates poorly to held-out data. Early stopping and other regularizers can prevent this degeneracy, but they are limited to selecting posterior approximations along an unfavorable optimization trajectory set by in-sample residuals, where the posterior mean is underfit while the posterior variance is overfit. To avoid this trade-off, we propose Cross-Fitting NPE (CF-NPE), which uses sample splitting to separate conditional-mean estimation from the estimation of the posterior's higher moments. Using $K$-fold cross-fitting, CF-NPE fits $K$ posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the resulting out-of-fold residuals. In experiments with synthetic data and in a cosmological application, CF-NPE achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE and typically improves calibration. CF-NPE is most useful in high-dimensional, simulation-limited settings.

papers.title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
papers.summary: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.

papers.title: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps
papers.summary: We develop a deep Pontryagin learning framework for high-dimensional continuous-time stochastic control problems that naturally accommodates jump-diffusions. In contrast to direct policy optimization, which repeatedly differentiates the objective through the entire time-discretized dynamics, our method separates adjoint learning from policy improvement by explicitly incorporating state-sensitivity information from the Pontryagin stochastic maximum principle. For a fixed Markov control, we first compute pathwise adjoint labels by backpropagating the reward through time along simulated state trajectories, and project these labels onto the Markov state through a supervised regression step. The control is then updated by enforcing the pointwise Hamiltonian stationarity condition. We prove that the resulting projected adjoint process satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges, as the time step tends to zero, to the solution of the corresponding continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy, stability, and scalability of the approach.

papers.title: SafeWall: A Risk-Aware Job Walltime Recommendation for HPC Scheduling
papers.summary: In high-performance computing (HPC), users must submit resource requirements for their jobs, with user-supplied walltime being a critical parameter. When user data is limited, the system employs statistical shrinkage to align these margins with a global baseline, ensuring robustness. This yields a lightweight mechanism that optimizes the trade-off between prediction accuracy and termination risk. SafeWall is modular and applicable to various learning-based prediction models. papers.title: A Fisher-Geometric View of Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.summary: Consolidating specialized foundation models into a unified generalist is a central goal of post-training. The program minimizes the worst per-domain residual and reports its energy-normalized values as the domain residual spectrum. Phase~2 lets this spectrum govern what may be added: RGBM passivates domains with low normalized residuals, trains isolated branches only for domains above the spectral gap, and writes back the admitted updates with calibrated shrinkage. papers.title: Parameterized Complexity of $L_p$-Lipschitz Constants for Input Convex Neural Networks and $L_p$-Norm Maximization over Zonotopes
papers.summary: Lipschitz constants are a standard way to quantify the sensitivity of neural networks to small input perturbations, but computing them is difficult even for shallow ReLU networks. These results resolve the corresponding questions regarding the parameterized complexity status for zonotope norm maximization and two-layer ICNN Lipschitz constants. papers.title: Time-Correlated Video Bridge Matching
papers.summary: Bridge Matching (BM) learns a stochastic transport between two data distributions and is therefore a natural tool for data-to-data tasks such as video frame interpolation, image-to-video generation, and video super-resolution. Existing bridge models for video, however, use a reference process that treats the frames of a clip independently, so temporal structure enters only through the network or the choice of the bridge endpoints. We propose Time-Correlated Video Bridge Matching (TCVBM), which places temporal structure into the reference process itself: the frames of a clip are coupled by a linear SDE whose drift is a discrete Laplacian along the time axis, and known frames enter as boundary conditions. The transition and bridge distributions remain Gaussian and available in closed form, so training and sampling are as simple as in standard BM, which is recovered in the limit of zero coupling. A spectral analysis shows that the prior damps high temporal frequencies, injects temporally smooth noise, and relaxes towards a boundary-determined profile, such as the linear interpolation between key frames. In controlled comparisons with frame-independent bridges under identical architectures and training budgets, TCVBM improves most automatic metrics for frame interpolation (Moving MNIST, UCF-101, Vimeo-90K) and image-to-video generation (Moving MNIST, UCF-101), e.g., reducing FVD from 688 to 611 for frame interpolation on UCF-101, and human raters prefer its frame interpolations for temporal consistency in 49$\%$ of comparisons versus 15$\%$ for the baseline ($p<10^{-17}$); for super-resolution, it performs on par with BM on automatic metrics.

papers.title: CTLite: Lightweight Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Reusable Continuous-Time Summaries

papers.title: Learning SOCP Solver Dynamics with Graph Neural Networks
papers.summary: Second-order cone programs (SOCPs) are a fundamental class of convex optimization problems widely applied across engineering domains. Classical interior-point methods are robust and accurate, but their iterative nature can be costly in real-time or repeated-solve settings. A shared GNN model is applied repeatedly, refining the current iterate at each step and enabling inference for a variable number of iterations. Rather than predicting the solution in a single pass, SOCPNet learns from intermediate iterates to progressively refine its estimates using a trajectory-regularized training procedure. Finally, we demonstrate how trained SOCPNet models can be used in a hybrid optimization pipeline by warm-starting a classical interior-point solver, reducing solver iterations without loss of accuracy.

papers.title: Trust Your Targets: Is Target Propagation Block-Diagonal Gauss-Newton?
papers.summary: Target propagation (TP) is a backpropagation alternative in which local targets carry the global learning signal. papers.title: Provable Adversarial Detection: Prime Quantization meets Gromov--Wasserstein

papers.summary: Generator--critic trading systems pair an LLM-based trader that makes trading decisions with a red team agent that evaluates these decisions and provides feedback for revision. However, improving individual trading decisions does not ensure that both agents learn from experience and improve together over time. This raises an important question: how can the trader and red-Team select useful experience and learn from each other's evolving behavior? On one hand, experience that benefits decisions under one market condition may become ineffective or harmful under another. On the other hand, trading outcomes reflect both agents' actions, making it difficult to derive appropriate experience for each role. In this work, we propose ACE-Trader, an adversarial co-evolution trading framework. Specifically, we first develop separate context-dependent memory selectors that learn to identify useful experience for the current trading decision. Both selectors receive shared feedback from net-return differences between complete memory-assisted and memory-free trading pipelines, with online updates emphasizing recent outcomes. We further design a co-evolution mechanism that links role-specific memories through shared trading records. We use these records to evaluate the Red-Team's risk assessments and the effects of the Trader's revisions against realized market outcomes, then derive experience for their respective memories. By linking this experience to the corresponding records, we enable the Trader to improve its proposals based on prior critiques and the Red-Team to adjust its review focus as the Trader's behavior changes. Experiments on U.S. stock trading show that ACE-Trader outperforms all 22 active baselines in cumulative return and achieves the highest Sharpe ratio and lowest maximum drawdown across both active methods and passive benchmarks.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Federated Domain Generalization in Edge Networks via Dynamic Prototype Regulation
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed paradigm for Internet of Things (IoT) edge networks. By employing a dual-parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) architecture, we design a channel-aware tiered transmission mechanism that adaptively truncates payloads to maximize node survival rates under fading conditions. To mitigate client drift, we introduce the Gradient-Conflict Aware Modulation (GCAM) mechanism. GCAM operates within the low-dimensional feature manifold to dynamically resolve multi-objective optimization conflicts with minimal edge computation latency, thereby reducing computation-induced network outages. papers.title: Sector-Ring Linear Reservoirs: Sector-Wise Decay-Timescale Allocation With State Reuse Across Candidate Settings
papers.summary: In reservoir computing, performance depends on whether the fixed dynamics of the reservoir suit the task, and the appropriate memory length and frequency response differ across tasks. The reservoir settings are found by a search on each task, and driving the reservoir with the input and collecting its states for every candidate setting dominates the cost of the search. In a reservoir with a linear recurrence, the dynamics decompose into modes, one per eigenvalue, and the eigenvalue distribution becomes a design variable. We propose the Sector-Ring Linear Reservoir (SRLR), in which the eigenvalue angles are fixed at evenly spaced positions around a circle and one decay timescale, chosen from a few values, is assigned to each sector of consecutive angles. To keep the scale of each mode's state equal across candidates, the input weights are scaled using the power spectrum of the training input. To reduce the cost of the search, the states of the modes for each decay-timescale value are computed once and reused across candidates. On prediction and reconstruction benchmarks built from chaotic systems, the SRLR achieved, in all eight cases, a lower mean test error than a reference model in which all modes share one decay timescale, and was competitive with nonlinear echo state network and leaky-integrator echo state network baselines. The selected decay-timescale profiles changed with the prediction target and horizon. The state reuse reduced the number of computed mode trajectories in the search by 99.8% relative to per-candidate recomputation.

papers.title: Fair Regression under Approximate Demographic Parity
papers.summary: Exact demographic parity requires the same prediction distribution across sensitive groups. In regression, this can be too restrictive and reduce predictive accuracy. We instead bound every pairwise Wasserstein distance between group-specific prediction distributions by a chosen tolerance, allowing the groups to differ while keeping fairness tunable. On the real line, the prediction and constrained transport problems have the same infimum. If the transport problem attains this value and suitable Monge maps exist, a deterministic transport-form predictor realizes it. Under a standard one-dimensional condition, the problem becomes a bounded quantile optimization that is convex when the conditional expected loss is convex in prediction. Under squared loss with two positively weighted groups, the $W_1$, $W_2$, and $W_\infty$ constraints yield soft-thresholding, shrinkage, and clipping. Under the stated conditions, we establish rates for the known-cost plug-in estimator. When the cost is unavailable, we describe an observed-loss computational proxy. Synthetic and California 2018 ACS studies illustrate the tunable fairness-accuracy trade-off and distinguish calibration feasibility from held-out fairness and accuracy.

papers.title: SparsePixels: Efficient Convolution for Sparse Data on FPGAs
papers.summary: Inference of standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on FPGAs often incurs high latency and a long initiation interval due to the deep nested loops required to densely convolve every input pixel regardless of its feature value. papers.title: Fundamental Limits of Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation with User Dropouts in Federated Learning
papers.summary: Secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of users' gradients or model updates without revealing individual values. With user dropouts, correlated random keys protect local gradients while allowing recovery of the desired gradient sum. We consider three phases: key distribution, masked-gradient upload, and mask elimination. Users establish correlated keys, upload masked gradients, and provide additional messages to eliminate residual aggregate masks. Existing information-theoretic schemes typically design mask-elimination communication for a prescribed dropout threshold and evaluate its cost under worst-case dropouts across the masked-gradient upload and mask-elimination phases. Such designs cannot adjust communication to actual dropout scenarios. Moreover, the randomness and communication costs of establishing correlated keys remain largely unexplored. To address these limitations, we formulate an adaptive secure aggregation framework under the T-colluding security constraint and construct a single scheme that supports all feasible dropout scenarios by adapting its communication to the actual number of dropouts. We establish converse bounds on four resources: key randomness, key-distribution communication, masked-gradient communication, and mask-elimination communication. The latter two bounds are characterized for each realized dropout set in the masked-gradient upload phase. The proposed scheme achieves the optimal masked-gradient communication rate for every feasible dropout scenario and the optimal mask-elimination communication rate in almost all feasible regimes. Its key rate and key-distribution communication rate are each optimal or within a factor of two of their respective information-theoretic optima. These results characterize the fundamental randomness and communication costs of secure aggregation with user dropouts.

papers.title: How Much Does One Wrong Answer Cost? Error Propagation in Constraint Pruning with Noisy LLM Oracles
papers.summary: Constraint pruning saves queries to a large language model (LLM) or another noisy oracle by skipping each yes/no question implied by answers accepted earlier, for example through transitivity. Entity-resolution systems and LLM-based rankers use this idea. However, their analyses typically assume a correct oracle. We argue that pruning should be judged by its risk when the oracle errs, since an accepted wrong answer spreads to every question it implies. When each answer is wrong independently with small probability $\varepsilon$, the first-order risk is set by how many facts one wrong answer corrupts on average. We consider two kinds of constraints. For implication rules, as in taxonomies, pruning in a random order adds no first-order risk: a wrong answer that would change $k$ facts is accepted with probability $1/k$, so it costs one fact on average. Rules with $s$ premises break this balance: a wrong answer at a premise shared by $r$ rules can cost order $r^{1-1/s}$ facts. For entity resolution with $m$ records of one entity, the first-order risk equals $\varepsilon$ times the Wiener index (the total pairwise distance) of the spanning tree built by the query order. Pivot orders, which first compare one record with all others, amplify errors by less than 2 and are optimal; random orders by order $m^{1/3}$; the common most-similar-first order is the worst in one dimension and, for large $m$, worse than random in two. With several entities, the cost of wrongly merging two does not depend on how many others exist. Simulations agree with every predicted constant within sampling error.

papers.title: Neural Video Coding under Limited Delay: Theoretical Optimality and System Design
papers.summary: Traditional neural video compression (NVC) methods predominantly follow strictly causal predictive-coding paradigm, treating zero-frame delay as a fixed constraint rather than delay as an explicit design parameter. In practice, we instantiate GFSC through lightweight neural modules, allowing existing causal predictive codecs to be augmented without modifying their core architectures. Experiments across multiple NVC models and datasets show that GFSC consistently improves rate-distortion performance over the corresponding causal counterparts. papers.title: Learning to Couple: Context-Adaptive Joint Denoising for Diffusion Language Models
papers.summary: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, but factorized denoisers treat simultaneous predictions as conditionally independent. We jointly optimize both components under a conditional denoising objective using a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters. papers.title: Interpretable time series analysis with Gumbel dynamics
papers.summary: Switching dynamical systems can model complicated time series data while maintaining interpretability by inferring a finite set of dynamics primitives and explaining different portions of the observed time series with one of these primitives. Furthermore, we apply our model to two real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to infer interpretable states in stochastic time series with multiple dynamics, a setting where traditional methods often fail.

papers.title: Sampling of Signals on Multigraphs: From Removable and Uniqueness sets to Spectral Proxies
papers.summary: In this paper, we study the sampling of bandlimited signals on multigraphs, where several graphs with different shift operators are defined on the same set of nodes. Since the shift operators do not commute in general, they admit only a joint block diagonalization, and the frequencies of the multigraph signal model are matrices rather than scalars. Relying on a formal algebraic convolutional signal model, we introduce a notion of frequency and bandwidth for multigraph signals that does not depend on any individual layer, and we extend the notions of removable and uniqueness sets to multigraphs. We prove that the optimality of a sampling set is determined exclusively by the common Fourier basis and its invariant subspaces, and not by any individual layer, although the individual layers provide computable sufficient conditions that certify a sampling set as a uniqueness set. Since identifying which layers provide reliable certificates requires spectral information, we propose an aggregate operator that pools the information of all the layers, is computable directly from the shift operators, and certifies uniqueness without any assumption on the individual layers. This operator leads to a greedy sampling algorithm that does not require computing the joint block diagonalization. Numerical experiments on multigraphs whose layers order the frequencies inconsistently show that the proposed algorithm selects better-conditioned sampling sets and attains lower reconstruction errors than single-layer methods.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Gated SHAP-Dirichlet Refinement for MRI-Based Depression Classification
papers.summary: Structural MRI-based classification of major depressive disorder (MDD) remains challenging due to subtle, heterogeneous anatomical changes. We propose uncertainty-gated SHAP-Dirichlet refinement, a post-hoc reliability layer that improves predictions without retraining the classifier. The method retrieves similar labeled SHAP explanations, constructs Dirichlet class evidence, and selectively refines uncertain predictions through probabilistic fusion, while allowing unreliable cases to be deferred for expert review. We evaluate five classifiers on 504 SRPBS subjects (252 controls and 252 MDD patients) using 159 anatomical features and repeated nested cross-validation. Refinement improved accuracy across all 8 repetitions for TabM and ResNet, yielding mean gains of 1.04 and 0.45 percentage points (sign test p=0.008), while modifying at most 8.3% of predictions. Gains were concentrated among low-confidence cases, with significant improvements in calibration. The method also benefited an RBF support vector machine but not logistic regression or random forests. Ablations confirmed the importance of uncertainty gating and soft fusion. Dirichlet evidence identified baseline errors (AUROC 0.62), while deferring 50% of cases increased retained-case accuracy to approximately 75%. These findings support selective explanation-guided refinement as a practical approach to improving prediction reliability and facilitating expert triage in MDD classification.

papers.title: Clean Forcing: Drift-Resistant Autoregressive Video Diffusion with a Frozen Base
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ~95% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model's own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces Δ-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to -0.16 with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57 with over 150x less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.

papers.title: Conditional Average Treatment Effect Distillation for Hypothetical State-Intervention Targeting Under Budget Constraints
papers.summary: Personalized public-health targeting must capture heterogeneous intervention benefits while remaining interpretable under resource constraints. Flexible causal-effect models can be hard to operationalize, while coarse subgroup policies may lose individualized effect information. We study budget-constrained hypothetical state interventions in observational data without a logged historical decision policy. For obesity, elevated glucose, and lifetime smoking-history states, causal-structure-informed pretreatment covariates are prespecified, with capacity capped at 70% of those observed in the adverse state. We evaluate causal distillation where Causal Forest and Bayesian Causal Forest teachers estimate conditional average treatment effects (CATEs), which decision tree and random forest students approximate. We compare individualized policies with unsupervised K-means subgroup policies and supervised causal-tree policies with leaf counts matched to K-means cluster counts. Observational policies are assessed on held-out data using a doubly robust estimator, bootstrap uncertainty, and decision-focused teacher-student fidelity measures. Across PIMA obesity and glucose and NHANES smoking-history experiments, each distilled student was within 0.011 absolute utility of its teacher, with allocation Jaccard similarities of 0.738-0.937. K-means and causal-tree policies were also competitive, with the highest point-estimate policy varying by application. Prespecified paired comparisons were nonsignificant after Holm adjustment, while near-budget-boundary agreement was less stable than global fidelity for some teacher-student pairs. Findings support causal distillation for translating flexible effect models into simpler budgeted targeting rules, although observational estimates depend on causal-identification assumptions and require longitudinal or prospective validation.

papers.title: CheXFuse: Guided Differential Joint Attention Fusion for Robust Multimodal Chest X-Ray Classification in Data-Scarce Medical Settings
papers.summary: A central challenge in multimodal learning is how to fuse modalities that differ substantially in predictive strength. When one modality provides a much stronger representation than another, indiscriminate cross-modal interaction can introduce weak, redundant, or unstable signals, limiting or even degrading performance relative to the strongest unimodal representation. To address this problem, we propose CheXFuse, a multimodal fusion framework based on Guided Differential Joint Attention (GuDJA). CheXFuse combines image and text token representations within a joint multimodal sequence, where learned token guidance emphasizes informative representations and differential attention reduces less useful attention responses. We evaluate CheXFuse on the Indiana University (IU) Chest X-ray dataset, using binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification as the downstream task. Experiments are conducted under both original-report and masked-report settings, with the latter serving as a controlled stress test under reduced textual informativeness. CheXFuse with GuDJA achieves the strongest mean overall performance across the evaluated baselines and ablations, reaching 95.73% accuracy, 95.79% F1-score, 96.54% recall, and 95.28% sensitivity at 95% specificity (Sens@95Spec) with original reports, and 95.58%, 95.60%, 95.60%, and 94.34%, respectively, under masked reports. These results suggest that GuDJA provides a promising fusion strategy under asymmetric or partially reduced modality informativeness.

papers.title: Mask-Aware Execution for Efficient JEPA Training
papers.summary: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are becoming a core representation-learning primitive and a building block for latent world models across vision, video, audio, brain dynamics, and time series. Despite (potential of) wide deployment, current JEPA training pipelines are inefficient: each input is executed through multiple mask-specific branches, with redundant target-side work, and memory-bound token routing. These costs grow with the number of masks and limit GPU efficiency. We present M-JEPA, a mask-aware execution architecture that restructures JEPA training without changing the learning objective. M-JEPA separates mask-independent computation from mask-dependent routing, enabling shared context encoder execution, fused token routing and slicing with backward support, sparse target encoder execution over the union of target tokens, and masked patch embedding for sparse inputs. The resulting pipeline preserves training semantics while reducing computation, memory traffic, and synchronization overhead. We implement M-JEPA for five JEPA variants and evaluate it on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Compared against the state-of-the-art baselines, M-JEPA achieves up to 1.7x end-to-end training speedup for 2-10 masks. Separately, with masked patch embedding, 4.75x patch-embedding speedup at high sparsity. These results show that execution restructuring, rather than changes to the JEPA objective, is a key lever for efficient JEPA training.

papers.title: Curriculum Learning Teaches LLMs Long-Horizon Implicit Reasoning, Up To A Limit
papers.summary: LLMs "reason" by externalizing intermediate steps as tokens through chain-of-thought (CoT), yet even frontier reasoning models hit abrupt performance cliffs on long-horizon tasks. Implicit reasoning (reasoning within a single forward pass) is useful during CoT generation, as the model can "search ahead" to decide the correct next move without explicit search. Models with weak implicit reasoning are more likely to commit to wrong paths and must attempt to recover via backtracking, while models with strong implicit reasoning identify the correct proof strategy directly, shortening the CoT. However, prior work shows LLMs struggle to reason implicitly beyond shallow depths, with no relief from scale. We investigate whether curriculum learning can extend this depth by fine-tuning on examples with progressively increasing vocabulary size and lookahead (the number of steps a model must search ahead to identify the correct next move). At matched compute, curriculum-trained models achieve lookaheads where no-curriculum training fails. Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98% accuracy on problems with lookahead up to 256 with curriculum, compared to 45% without. However, progress slows as fine-tuning continues, following a saturating exponential that suggests a maximum intrinsic lookahead to which models can learn to reason implicitly. Larger models reach higher fitted ceilings, fine-tuning pretrained models far outpaces training from scratch, and curriculum step sizes that are too large stall progression. Finally, the capability acquired on synthetic data transfers to natural language reasoning, with curriculum-trained models outperforming models trained without curriculum at matched compute on 11 natural language reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Smooth Flow Matching for Synthesizing Functional Data
papers.summary: Functional data, i.e., random functions observed over a continuous domain, are increasingly available in areas such as biomedical research, health informatics, and epidemiology. However, effective statistical analysis for functional data is often hindered by challenges such as privacy constraints, sparse and irregular sampling, infinite-dimensionality, and non-Gaussian structures. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework named Smooth Flow Matching (SFM), tailored for generative modeling of functional data that enables statistical analysis without exposing sensitive real data. Under a copula framework, SFM constructs a semiparametric smooth flow to generate infinite-dimensional functional data, free of Gaussianity and low-rank assumptions. It is computationally efficient, handles irregular observations, and guarantees the smoothness of the generated functions, offering a practical and flexible solution in scenarios where existing deep generative methods are not applicable. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the advantages of SFM in terms of both synthetic data quality and computational efficiency. We then apply SFM to generate clinical trajectory data from the MIMIC-IV patient electronic health records (EHR) longitudinal database. Our analysis showcases the ability of SFM to produce high-quality surrogate data for downstream tasks, highlighting its potential to boost the utility of EHR data for clinical applications.

papers.title: PRISM: Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling to Enhance Solubility OOD Generalization
papers.summary: Solubility depends on intermolecular interactions between solutes and solvents, and is central to drug discovery, chemical and materials process engineering. Its prediction requires out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization to unseen solutes, solvents, and solvent mixtures, where supervised methods suffer from data scarcity, and existing self-supervised methods do not explicitly learn chemically meaningful relations. Learning chemically meaningful relational information without labels can alleviate data scarcity and improve OOD generalization, but remains challenging. We introduce Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling (PRISM) and apply it to solubility OOD generalization. PRISM is a label-free pretraining framework that converts expert-defined chemical priors into relational teachers. For solubility prediction, it trains four encoders to preserve the population-level relational information from priors capturing hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural effects, using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to match distance-based neighborhood distributions during pretraining. Across scaffold, solute, and solvent OOD settings, PRISM matches or surpasses supervised and self-supervised baselines. Under mixed-solvent OOD, freezing the four PRISM encoders and training a lightweight fusion-and-composition head outperforms strong baselines and substantially reduces run-to-run variation. Ablations and control studies confirm that gains stem from chemically meaningful relational structures baked into the encoders by PRISM. We expect this strategy of turning relational priors into self-supervision signals to extend beyond solubility prediction to domains where chemically or biologically meaningful relational priors are available.

papers.title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
papers.summary: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by 17.6% (WS-21) and 17.0% (Mean-$L_1$), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from $3.1\times$ to $2.3\times$. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population-rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.

papers.title: Text Dominance in Paralinguistic Conflict: Tracing Suppression Through Audio LLM Circuits
papers.summary: Audio LLMs deployed in settings such as crisis hotlines and customer support are only useful beyond speech-to-text pipelines if they use acoustic cues rather than the transcript alone. We test whether they prioritise transcript content over paralinguistic cues (emotion, speaker identity, sarcasm) and trace the mechanism when they do. Across six audio LLMs under LISTEN-style conflict conditions, the mean text-dominance rate on mismatched text+audio items is 0.78 (0.86 excluding sarcasm). In the most text-dominant screened model, probing shows speaker identity remains linearly decodable at ceiling at the language model's input, so the failure is not perceptual. Back-patching, reported to repair lexical text dominance, has no measurable effect here; but it also fails on its own source task in our replication (n=300), so we treat its null as uninformative rather than as evidence of non-transfer. Attention knockout partially restores audio-grounded output by blocking the claim from propagating through intermediate tokens during open-ended generation, whereas blocking the answer position's direct connection to the conflicting claim has no effect. The claim's influence therefore travels through an intermediate relay rather than a single severable edge. The effect appears only in free-form generation and not in closed-set multiple choice, suggesting that benchmarks relying on that format may be systematically blind to interventions of this kind. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/AdvayRoongta/audio-llm-mech-interp.

papers.title: Cognitive Map in Large Language Models
papers.summary: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.

papers.title: Compute Allocation in Bilinear Contrastive Representation Learning via Scaling Laws
papers.summary: Efficient reasoning systems increasingly rely on large contrastive representation models for multimodal retrieval, grounding, and decision-making. However, under a limited compute budget, it is unclear how to allocate resources among representation dimension, paired data, and optimization steps. We study this question in a sketched bilinear contrastive-learning model. Under a paired Gaussian latent-variable setup, we derive a risk decomposition into irreducible risk, approximation error, GD bias, GD variance, and a cross term. The resulting scaling law shows that contrastive learning differs from standard linear regression because the effective degrees of freedom are pairs of spectral directions rather than single directions. This product effective dimension determines how finite-sample noise grows with optimization time. Most importantly, using the compute proxy $\mathcal C \asymp LNM^2$, we derive compute-allocation rules balancing model size, data, and training time. To the best of our knowledge, our result provides the first theoretical backbone for resource allocation in contrastive representation learning through provable scaling laws.

papers.title: Linear RNN Scaling Laws: When Longer Sequences Beat More Sequences
papers.summary: Empirical scaling laws for autoregressive language models relate prediction loss to model size, data size, and optimization compute, but their theoretical origin is still poorly understood in sequential pretraining settings. We study this question in a tractable teacher--student model where a stable latent linear RNN generates trajectories and a sketched linear recurrent student is trained by safeguarded full-batch WSD gradient descent on next-token prediction. The sketch dimension $M$ plays the role of model size, while $N$ independent trajectories of length $P$ provide the training tokens. We allow the innovation and initialization covariances to have different power-law exponents $α$ and $θ$. The induced design spectrum produces explicit approximation, optimization, and statistical scaling laws separated by spectral crossovers. When $θ\geα$, the original one-scale rates $M^{1-β_α}$, $R^{(1-β_α)/α}$, and $(NP)^{-1}\min\{M,R^{1/α}\}$ are recovered. When $α-2r\leθ<α$, the heavier initialization tail changes the rates beyond $P$-dependent model and optimization crossovers. The proof uses a covariance event only internally and a globally safeguarded step size on its complement. The variance retains the factor $(NP)^{-1}$, while sequence length also suppresses the initialization transient, so $N$ and $P$ cease to be fully interchangeable in the two-scale regime.

papers.title: Predictable Failure in Multi-Hop Retrieval: Score-Distributional Confidence Scoring and Abstention
papers.summary: Multi-hop retrieval failures are not uniformly distributed across queries: they cluster in structurally predictable subpopulations. We prove two results formalizing this structure. First (CWAR Reducibility): confident-failure reduction is achievable if and only if retrieval features carry mutual information about success, a condition satisfied by LLM-judge pipelines but substantially weaker in dense-only settings, explaining the AUC-AC gap between regimes. Second (Feature Regime Complementarity): no single ANN score feature achieves best predictive performance across all failure regimes; the dominant feature differs between datasets (query length on MuSiQue, hop-1 concentration on HoVer), and a constructive witness pair shows each is necessary in one regime and non-contributory in the other. We instantiate these principles in RegimeAbstain, which computes a Retrieval Confidence Score (RCS), a logistic function of up to nine query-ANN structural features, all available without any additional LLM call, and uses it to implement a calibrated abstention policy. We define the Confident-Wrong-Answer Rate (CWAR) metric and evaluate across three multi-hop benchmarks (MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, HoVer) and two retrieval architectures (LLM-judge and dense-only), covering five failure regimes with CWAR from 14.5% to 62.1%. RCS achieves best or co-best AUC-AC in all five conditions against eight confidence baselines. On MuSiQue (LLM-judge), RCS reduces CWAR from 39.5% to 20.6% at 50% coverage (47.8% relative reduction), with ECE=0.035. A model trained on MuSiQue transfers to 2WikiMultiHopQA with only -0.5pp AUC loss, confirming the domain-agnostic structure of regime features.

papers.title: Bandit Learning in General Open Multi-agent Systems
papers.summary: Open systems, where agents arrive and depart over time, are growing in digital platforms. Existing work on online learning in such systems, however, often relies on structural assumptions that may be restrictive in practice. In particular, heterogeneous rewards and general agent patterns create three new challenges: arrivals induce endogenous non-stationarity, agent patterns govern the rate of information accumulation, and uncertainty brought by new agents accumulates over time and scales regret. To this end, we formulate a learning problem for open systems that accommodates both forms of generality. We introduce new concepts to capture the inherent complexities: the \emph{pre-training degree} of new agents quantifies how much information an agent carries upon entry, \emph{stability} measures the impact of population changes on the global optimum, and \emph{global dynamic regret} compares the cumulative expected reward with that of the varying optimal arms. We also study a manifold representation of agents and introduce a \emph{dynamic population embedding} that directly encodes the population functional for each arm. We develop two UCB-based methods. The first combines entry information with online observations through agent-wise confidence bounds and aggregates the estimates and uncertainties for arm selection. The second pools agent-level observations through kernel regression on the manifold and constructs UCBs by projecting the confidence sets onto the current population embedding. Entry uncertainty enters the regret linearly through the pre-training error, while in stable regimes, regret is governed by the time needed to identify the stable optimal arm. With the manifold as a handle, regret is governed by the information gained from agent representations. These bounds all depend on population dynamics, but in different ways.

papers.title: CVTA: Cross-Variable Temporal Attention for Multivariate Irregular Time Series Prediction
papers.summary: Irregularly sampled multivariate time series arise in many real-world domains such as healthcare, climate science, and large-scale monitoring systems. In this work, we introduce Cross-Variable Temporal Attention (CVTA), a short-term, continuous-time forecasting framework that learns prediction functions from its compact, interpretable state summarizing recent temporal dynamics across variables. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CVTA can be integrated as an auxiliary module into existing state-of-the-art prediction models through a dynamic meta-decision model. papers.title: Reward and Behavioral Measures of LLM Coordination in Dining Philosophers
papers.summary: Does high reward indicate productive coordination among language-model agents sharing resources? The reward decomposition explains this mismatch: avoiding deadlock earns a bonus without requiring meal production. papers.title: Finite Interaction Lens: Structured Precision Sharing for Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: Identifying which visual interventions interact in a vision-language model requires comparing their joint and separate effects. The resulting four-output difference can be small enough for rounding error to obscure it. We introduce the Finite Interaction Lens (FIL), a mixed-precision method for evaluating finite intervention families. At each selected linear projection, FIL decomposes each candidate's input into a native state, two single-intervention components, and a full-dimensional mixed residual. It projects the single-intervention components at higher precision and reuses the same numerical contributions in the joint candidates, while retaining every mixed residual and nonlinear trajectory. We derive a local cancellation identity and a conditional bound on error propagation through a smooth nonlinearity. In one MLP of Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, FIL reduces final interaction MSE by 94.4% on 16 synthetic families and by 99.85% and 99.35% in two separate four-image COCO studies, relative to a control that has the same nominal BF16-product budget and higher-precision single interventions but projects each joint candidate independently. One image accounts for most of the absolute gain in each COCO study. Higher-accuracy multi-product BF16 arithmetic on all candidates gives lower aggregate error at similar total query times. Single-product BF16 already recovers the reference choices in both candidate-selection tasks we tested. On these development inputs, FIL improves interaction fidelity at a fixed nominal precision budget. Its practical value depends on a task that needs the extra fidelity.

papers.title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena

papers.title: Convex Compositional Reasoning Models
papers.summary: Compositional energy-based models can generalize to larger combinatorial reasoning problems by reusing a learned factor energy across many local constraints. In our paper, we show that a key bottleneck in compositional reasoning is not composition itself, but the non-convex geometry of the learned energy landscape. To solve this problem, we introduce Convex Compositional Energy Minimization (CCEM), a framework that parameterizes each factor with an input-convex neural network and optimizes the composed energy over a tight convex relaxation of the feasible set. Because convexity is preserved under summation, the global relaxed objective remains convex, enabling deterministic projected first-order optimization. CCEM is trained in two stages: factor-level contrastive learning to shape local energy basins, followed by end-to-end refinement through an unrolled projected solver. Our experiments show that our models trained on small subproblems or a single problem size transfer to larger instances without retraining.

papers.title: FTFM: Factorized Tabular Foundation Models
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are becoming a powerful alternative to conventional tabular learning, adapting to new datasets in context without task-specific training. Current architectures, however, face a trade-off: models that preserve cell-level representations are expensive because they repeatedly attend across rows and columns, while faster models collapse each row into a fixed embedding and lose this fine-grained state. We introduce Factorized Tabular Foundation Models (FTFM), which preserve cell representations while factorizing their computation through one contextual latent per row and one per column. Cells no longer attend to one another directly; instead, each cell is updated through the interaction of its row and column latents, reducing repeated attention while retaining feature-specific information. FTFM achieves competitive predictive performance in tabular classification on major benchmarks such as TabArena and BeyondArena.

papers.title: LandscapeSHAP: Which Persistent Homology Class Gets the Credit?
papers.summary: Shapley values, a solution concept from cooperative game theory, have recently become a standard tool for feature credit allocation in machine learning. Because each landscape coordinate is a rank statistic, crediting a model's prediction back to individual persistent homology classes (persistence diagram points) is nontrivial. For linear models on persistence landscapes, LandscapeSHAP has a closed form expression that gives the exact Shapley value of every persistence diagram point. In particular, there is no coalition sampling required. We further prove that the four Shapley "fairness" axioms uniquely characterize this credit allocation for any model, not only linear ones. For a general nonlinear model, this unique value can only be calculated exactly from its defining coalition averaging formula, which requires considering all $2^N$ many coalitions, where $N$ is the number of points in the persistence diagram. This is computationally intractable for persistence diagrams of realistic size. We complement the exact linear model result with an efficient Monte Carlo sampling of persistence diagram coalitions. We give convergence rates in terms of number of samples needed to approximate to a desired degree of accuracy. We also prove stability results for the LandscapeSHAP credit allocation, for any model.

papers.title: Paloma: Phase-Conditioned Residual Modulation for Time Series Forecasting
papers.summary: Explicitly modeling periodicity has proven to be an efficient approach for time series forecasting, where the residual, obtained after removing the periodic component from the time series, is typically treated as unstructured noise. Extensive experiments on twelve datasets demonstrate that Paloma achieves state-of-the-art and robust forecasting performance. Additional results show that the Paloma technique consistently improves a wide range of baseline models, validating its effectiveness as a general-purpose component. papers.title: Follow the Mixed Groups: Ridge-Tracking Gaussian Sampling for Zero-Variance Web Rollouts
papers.summary: Group relative policy optimization learns from a question only when the sampled responses disagree. The sampling weight is the marginal of a Gaussian target under a Gaussian approximation of that posterior, divided by a prediction of tool-call cost. In light of the increasing popularity of this approach, an important question is whether token-decoding explainability is an inherent property of transformers that should be expected to hold across architectures, scales, and training objectives, or merely an artifact of some implicit bias. We find that while some models indeed exhibit aligned and interpretable token decodings, others exhibit either inverted explainability maps or a complete lack of correlation with the image semantics. As we show, these tendencies toward different explainability behaviors are not intrinsic to the architecture and can vary arbitrarily with changes in the optimization landscape. We provide theoretical support for these observations by demonstrating a setting where a single fixed toy transformer architecture can provably implement the optimal classification rule in multiple ways, which differ in their patch-decoding explainability patterns. Our results show that token-decoding explainability is not an inherent property of trained transformers, but rather an outcome contingent on the problem setting and thus should not be a-priori assumed to hold. papers.summary: This book offers a hands-on introduction to building and understanding federated learning (FL) systems. papers.title: Improving the Expressive Power of Hybrid Sequence Models via Multi-Hop Retrieval
papers.summary: Hybrid architectures offer a promising approach to efficient language modeling by combining a small number of full-attention layers with a larger number of efficient sequence layers, such as sparse attention and recurrent layers. papers.title: A probability calibrator for machine-learning classifiers
papers.summary: In fields such as medicine and drug discovery, the ultimate goal of a classification is not to guess a class, but to choose the optimal course of action among a set of possible ones, usually not in one-one correspondence with the set of classes. This decision-theoretic problem requires proper probabilities for the classes. Proper probabilities conditional on the features are computationally almost impossible to find in many important cases. The main idea of the present work is to calculate probabilities conditional not on the features, but on the trained classifier's output. This calculation is cheap, needs to be made only once, and provides an output-to-probability "calibrator" or "transducer" that can be applied to all future outputs of the classifier. In conjunction with problem-dependent utilities, the probabilities of the transducer allow us to find the optimal choice among the classes or among a set of more general decisions, by means of expected-utility maximization. This idea is demonstrated in a simplified drug-discovery problem with a highly imbalanced dataset. The transducer and utility maximization together always lead to improved results, sometimes close to theoretical maximum, for all sets of problem-dependent utilities. The one-time-only calculation of the transducer also provides, automatically: (i) a quantification of the uncertainty about the transducer itself; (ii) the expected utility of the augmented algorithm (including its uncertainty), which can be used for algorithm selection; (iii) the possibility of using the algorithm in a "generative mode", useful if the training dataset is biased.

papers.title: Graph Partitioning with Demands: Generalized Conductance and its Applications
papers.summary: We study various graph partitioning tasks subject to general demands. In Graph Partitioning with Demands (GPD), the goal is to delete minimum cost supply edge set so that each remaining component contains at most a prescribed fraction of the total demand. On supply trees, we show that GC can be solved exactly in polynomial time. Recently, the work of Goujaud et al. [Math. Program. (2025)] made progress regarding acceleration in the context of smooth, strongly convex minimization: for a small enough inverse condition number, either the method does not accelerate on quadratics, or there exists a smooth strongly convex function such that heavy-ball cycles over the roots of unity. The constructed functions have two variables, thus leaving the question of acceleration over univariate functions open. In this work, we use a Fourier-based analysis to i) provide a proof for the non-acceleration of the heavy-ball method over the class of univariate smooth strongly convex functions. We also ii) provide a strict enlargement of the previous root-of-unity cycling region, with insights regarding the "fractional" sets of Goujaud et al. papers.title: A Transport Geometry of Benign Overfitting
papers.summary: Benign overfitting, the phenomenon that interpolating noisy data can be statistically harmless, is usually characterized through effective-rank conditions on the covariance spectrum. These conditions are fragile: a perturbation of vanishing relative operator and Frobenius norm can turn a benign covariance into one whose minimum-norm interpolator has non-vanishing excess risk. We argue that the natural geometry of benign overfitting is optimal transport of the log-eigenvalues, measured in units of the sample size $n$. In log-spectral coordinates, the deterministic equivalent of the risk becomes a functional of two measures smoothed by a logistic kernel centred at the interpolation threshold $\logκ$. We compute its exact first variation: the threshold moves by a sensitivity-weighted average of the log-eigenvalue displacements, and the influence of each eigenvalue decays exponentially with its log-distance to the threshold. We then derive global, dimension-free stability bounds. The variance functional is $8/(27n)$-Lipschitz in the 1-Wasserstein distance between log-spectra, with a sharp constant, and is controlled more generally by a threshold-localized transport discrepancy; an analogous bound controls the bias. Consequently, any rank-$k$ update of the covariance, of arbitrary norm, changes the variance functional by at most $3k/n$, and benign overfitting survives every perturbation whose localized transport cost is $o(n)$. The results extend to ridge regression and to infinite-dimensional trace-class covariances. Matching lower bounds show that the $n$-scaling is necessary and cannot be replaced by operator norms, Frobenius norms, or dimension-normalized spectral distances. Simulations, one-step feature learning in two-layer networks, and random features of real images support the theory and delineate its limits.

papers.title: PAAC: Privacy-Aware Agentic Device-Cloud Collaboration

papers.title: Integrable building blocks for symplectic neural networks: learned-type layers, fiber-preserving layers, and what a single layer can do
papers.summary: Exactly symplectic neural networks are built almost exclusively from shear maps and gain expressivity only through depth. We ask what else a single explicit symplectic layer can be. On nonlinear Schrödinger lattices with six to forty sites, twist layers alternating with linear symplectic maps are over a hundred times more accurate than every shear-based network, and with an on-site potential of learned form three to four orders of magnitude more accurate. On chains of Tao oscillators with the step size as an input, stretch layers are 45 to 70 times more accurate than learned-plane shears and recover the Hamiltonian to 1%. papers.title: Decentralized Online Exp-Concave Optimization
papers.summary: Decentralized Online Convex Optimization (D-OCO) is a fundamental framework in which a set of local agents aims to minimize a sequence of global loss functions using only local computations and communications. papers.title: Conjugate Compilation: Self-Improving Agentic Co-Compilation for Speculative Decoding
papers.summary: As LLM adoption surges, scaling model serving requires unlocking stranded GPU capacity alongside deploying more GPUs. papers.title: Double-Take: Improving Capacity, Binding, and Selectivity In Long-Context Within Bidirectional Memory

papers.title: Optimizing Prompt Sequences using Monte Carlo Tree Search for LLM-Based Optimization
papers.summary: Mathematical optimization is a core tool in engineering, operations research, and data science, but modeling real problems remains difficult and time-consuming. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) then explores and refines Reasoning Decomposition Plans (RDPs) prior to code synthesis, balancing exploration and exploitation across alternative plan sequences. Each candidate plan is rolled out into executable code, executed, and scored with an execution-grounded evaluator measuring executability, constraint satisfaction, and solution quality; this feedback is backpropagated through the search tree to guide subsequent search. papers.title: Distribution-Based Regularization for Reward Fine-Tuning Diffusion and Flow Models

papers.title: Statistical Inference and Learning for Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP)
papers.summary: The SHAP (short for Shapley additive explanation) framework has become an essential tool for attributing importance to variables in predictive tasks. While the explanations offered by SHAP are local by nature, learners often need global measures of feature importance in order to improve model explainability and perform feature selection. The most common approach for converting these local explanations into global ones is to compute either the mean absolute SHAP or mean squared SHAP. In this paper, we take a semi-parametric approach for calibrating confidence in estimates of the $p$th powers of Shapley additive explanations. We show that, by treating the SHAP curve as a nuisance function that must be estimated from data, one can reliably construct asymptotically normal estimates of the $p$th powers of SHAP. When $p \geq 2$, we show a de-biased estimator that combines U-statistics with Neyman orthogonal scores for functionals of nested regressions is asymptotically normal. When $1 \leq p < 2$ (and the hence target parameter is not twice differentiable), we construct de-biased U-statistics for a smoothed alternative. In particular, we show how to carefully tune the temperature parameter of the smoothing function in order to obtain inference for the true, unsmoothed $p$th power. papers.title: Query-Dependent Reading for Quantized Inner-Product Estimation: A Minimax Separation
papers.summary: We study quantization for inner-product estimation when storage and reading have separate budgets. In the static bit-probe model [Yao, 1981], an encoder stores $w$ bits about $x$ before seeing a query $y$, and a reader probes at most $r<w$ bits to estimate $x^\top y$. Both vectors lie in the $d$-dimensional Euclidean unit ball. Protocols may be randomized, and computation is unrestricted. Performance is measured by $d$ times the worst-case mean-squared error over $x,y$, averaged over protocol randomness. First, we show that query-independent reading cannot benefit from extra storage. Any such reader is equivalent to fully reading an $r$-bit message, even when later reads depend on previously returned bits. At fixed positive rates $W=w/d$ and $R=r/d$, the normalized minimax error converges to $1/(4^R-1)$, independent of $W$. The upper bound was already known [Ordentlich and Polyanskiy, 2025]. We prove the matching lower bound for arbitrary scalar decoders, extending the result for unbiased compressors [Safaryan et al., 2020]. Then, we show that query-dependent reading makes extra storage useful. We construct a two-batch protocol using Gaussian projections and random thresholds, with asymptotic normalized error at most $(π+o(1))/[4R\log(W/R)]$ as $W/R\to\infty$. At fixed $R$, this error vanishes as storage grows, giving an unbounded advantage over query-independent reading. We also prove a finite-dimensional lower bound for arbitrary encoders, decoders, and fully branching readers. In the doubly sparse regime $W/R\to\infty$ and $R\log(W/R)\to0$, it gives normalized error at least $(1-o(1))/[2R\log(W/R)]$. Thus, our protocol is optimal within a factor of $π/2$ in the leading constant.

papers.title: The Dichotomy Between Pattern Recognition and Step-by-Step Reasoning
papers.summary: We argue that pattern recognition and step-by-step reasoning are two ends of a spectrum. A large language model (LLM) learns to reason step-by-step when data is structured such that the next token depends on a small amount of preceding context. Inference in LLMs resembles pattern recognition when the next token depends on a large amount of preceding context. If the next token depends on only the $c$ most recent tokens, reasoning traces are paths on a De Bruijn graph whose nodes are $c$-length contexts and edges are next-token transitions between contexts. The set of reasoning traces of a task forms a directed acyclic subgraph of the De Bruijn graph. An LLM that has learned all edges of this subgraph can compose them to solve longer, unseen tasks, i.e., it reasons step-by-step. We prove that the number of edges is vanishingly small compared to the number of reasoning traces. Empirically, the number of training samples a transformer needs is a power law in the number of edges, so learning to reason step-by-step is sample efficient. We can induce De Bruijn structure in any task by maintaining a ``state'' that makes future reasoning independent of the past. The frequency of states in the reasoning trace determines $c$. We show, by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct to solve equations and answer questions about stories, that frequent states (small $c$) result in higher accuracy but greater fragility to perturbations at test time. LLMs trained with a large $c$ are only as good as models that perform pattern recognition without reasoning. A moderate density of states balances accuracy and robustness. We show that real-world data has De Bruijn structure: Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B retain over 75% of their accuracy on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond when attention is restricted to a sliding window less than 15% as long as the full reasoning trace.

papers.title: An Impossibility Result for ETF Target Geometry, and an Equinorm Remedy for Imbalanced Analytic Continual Learning
papers.summary: Analytic continual learning (ACL) methods such as ACIL and GACL fit a ridge-regression classifier head on frozen features via the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, achieving exemplar-free, exact updates. Equiangular geometry, by contrast, is exactly inert on the target side but actively harmful on the weight side, usually losing to plain one-hot. Hence, the generally useful part of Neural Collapse geometry in Analytic Continual Learning is equinorm post-processing of the weights, becoming more useful as class imbalance grows; and equiangularity is at best a no-op and induces catastrophic forgetting at worst.

papers.title: A Statistical Viewpoint on Adam, Shampoo and Muon

papers.title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts

papers.title: RF-GPT: Teaching AI to See the Wireless World

papers.title: From Overparameterised Expressions to Parsimonious Models: Fisher-Geometric Pruning for Symbolic Regression
papers.summary: Genetic programming symbolic regression (GPSR) often returns expressions that are larger than necessary, with dormant branches and finely tuned algebraic configurations that fit sampling noise. papers.title: How Does Muon Work in Private Deep Learning? Scalable Differentially Private Training via Orthogonalization

papers.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
papers.summary: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so loop survival under any sampler can be computed exactly from one forward pass. Pure sampling leaves a positive escape probability at every step; top-$p$ with threshold $π>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $π$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis predicts a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $λb^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 66\% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 1\% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 109 loops that survive DRY have $g\le 7$. We propose DRY-C, which adds a term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window. With it, none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the length limit, and task completion stayed close to DRY's.

papers.title: Attention over noisy examples: generalization and memorization in the exponential Hopfield network
papers.summary: In Hebbian learning from examples, a Hopfield network retrieves archetypes seen only through noisy examples. We study it in the exponential Hopfield model: one softmax attention step with the unlabelled examples as keys. At high temperature the archetype is lost in the crosstalk; at low temperature the softmax freezes on the closest training example, as in a random energy model, and the layer memorizes. In between, in a window widening with the square root of the network size, the layer pools the examples of the correct class and retrieves the unseen archetype as well as their majority vote allows, at any fixed load. papers.title: Optimal hypersurface decision trees
papers.summary: Optimal decision trees have attracted increasing attention in recent years, yet existing algorithms face two closely related challenges. First, the trees they construct have limited expressivity because their splitting rules are typically restricted to axis-parallel splits or binary features. Second, these algorithms generally scale poorly to large datasets. Its structure is naturally amenable to vectorization and parallelization, enabling efficient execution on GPUs, and the generic algorithm design can be used to accelerate other ODT variants, such as axis-parallel decision (ADT) trees. We further develop a safe pruning strategy that substantially reduces the number of candidate configurations and an incremental generation procedure that reduces the associated feasibility-checking cost from $O(K^2)$ to $O(K)$.

papers.title: When Should an In-Context Learner Expand Its Hypothesis Space?
papers.summary: Learning systems adapt quickly inside a familiar family of models. The harder step comes earlier: deciding, from observations that could be noise, an exception, a change within the family or structure outside it, whether opening a richer family is worth its cost. We treat this as a costly sequential decision: prediction failure must be turned into structural evidence, evidence into a value of expansion, and value into action. The Structural Revision Environment produces matched failures from each source, varies the price of expansion and the remaining horizon independently of the evidence, and admits exact Bayesian calculations and an exact normative solution of the one-shot decision. Its solution shows that revision is a value boundary and not an evidence threshold: one history has different optimal actions under different prices, horizons and announced queries, the boundary between local repair and expansion is set by the inputs a rule predicts and a repair cannot cover, and belief in the richer family crosses long before the decision does. Transformers trained in the environment reproduce this boundary from utility alone. Language models of three post-training lineages carry a failure-sensitive signal in their predictions that is not reflected in their revision decisions, and given the gain of expanding they read it without weighing it against price and horizon. Three models allowed to reason weigh the stated gain in the reference's proportions and still do not turn the history into an estimate of what expansion would buy. Controlled post-training of the meta-trained learners moves the prior and the sharpness of predictions, and neither moves the criterion.

papers.title: VBO-MI: A Differentiable Black-Box Optimization Framework via Variational Mutual Information Estimation
papers.summary: Many real-world tasks require optimizing expensive black-box functions accessible only through noisy evaluations, a setting commonly addressed with Bayesian optimization. papers.title: Encoder-Decoder Manifold Alignment for Idempotent Generation
papers.summary: Recently, several learning paradigms have been introduced to enforce idempotency in generative models. The goal of this property is to ensure that repeated application of a model leaves samples unchanged once they lie on the target data manifold. We argue that a key reason for the failure of generative models on some tasks, such as editing, is a geometric mismatch between the manifolds learned by the encoder and decoder. The encoder projects inputs onto one latent manifold, while the decoder implicitly learns to reconstruct data from a different manifold. This discrepancy prevents the model from learning truly idempotent mappings. To address this issue, we propose a new training framework that explicitly closes this gap by forcing the encoder and decoder to learn consistent representations of the same underlying data manifold. By aligning the geometry of these components, our method encourages stable projections. Empirically, we show that our approach achieves significantly lower idempotency error and consistently regenerates identical outputs under repeated application, compared to existing methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework on both image generation and image editing tasks. Finally, we show that enforcing idempotency in this manner improves identity preservation and information stability, leading to more realistic and controllable generative editing models.

papers.title: SPRINT: Stochastic Performative Prediction With Variance Reduction
papers.summary: Performative prediction (PP) is an algorithmic framework for optimizing machine learning (ML) models where the model's deployment affects the distribution of the data it is trained on. However, this latest progress is still based on the restricted bounded variance assumption in stochastic gradient estimates and yields convergence bounds with a non-vanishing error neighborhood that scales with the variance. This limitation motivates us to improve convergence rates and reduce error in stochastic optimization for PP, particularly in non-convex settings. Thus, we propose a new algorithm called stochastic performative prediction with variance reduction (SPRINT) and establish its convergence to an SPS solution at a rate of $O(1/T)$. Notably, the resulting error neighborhood is independent of the variance of the stochastic gradients. Experiments on multiple real datasets with non-convex models demonstrate that SPRINT outperforms SGD-GD in both convergence rate and stability.

papers.title: The Certification Exponent: Instance-Optimal Sequential Certification of Policy Improvement from History Dependent Logs
papers.summary: Before a new policy replaces a deployed one, we often want a certificate, computed from logged episodes, that it is better.
