papers.title: Platonic Projection Structures: Operator-Induced Observability in Representation Learning
papers.summary: We characterize observability in representation learning through Platonic Projection Structures (PPS), an operator-theoretic framework for analyzing representation accessibility under partial observation. Rather than treating observable outputs as direct reflections of latent representations, PPS models observation through a self-adjoint positive semidefinite operator acting on a latent representation space. A system is represented as a triple $(H, Π, O)$, where $H$ is a latent representation space, $Π\succeq 0$ is an observation operator, and $O(v)=\langle v,Πv\rangle$ defines an induced scalar observable. Observability is characterized by the quotient geometry $H/\ker(Π)$, representing equivalence classes of latent states indistinguishable under observation. We show that quantum measurement and representation inference under linear observation models share this operator-theoretic structure while differing in the algebraic properties of their observation operators; the correspondence is structural rather than physical. Representation transfer and knowledge distillation can likewise be interpreted as approximate preservation of observable geometry through $ΦΠ_T \approx Π_S Φ$. PPS also reveals a structural limitation of output-based interpretability: latent components in $\ker(Π)$ are inaccessible from induced observables, imposing intrinsic constraints on attribution and explanation methods. Controlled empirical validations demonstrate kernel-invariant observability, projection-induced attribution gaps, and rank-controlled observable geometry in latent representation spaces. PPS thus provides an explicit characterization of observability through operator-induced quotient geometry and a unified perspective on representation accessibility, interpretability, and projection-mediated inference.

papers.title: Is Flow Matching Just Trajectory Replay for Sequential Data?
papers.summary: Flow matching (FM) is increasingly used in scientific domains for time series generation and forecasting, where data often arise from underlying dynamical systems. This characterization provides an interpretable view of neural FM models as parametric estimation of an underlying nonparametric target and naturally leads to FreeFM: a closed-form, training-free realization of this target. papers.title: State-Matched Sequence Conformal Prediction
papers.summary: Sequential conformal prediction needs to decide which past errors should calibrate uncertainty for the current target. papers.title: From Mixing to Tearing: Graph Decomposition in Decentralized Optimization via Message Passing
papers.summary: We study decentralized minimization of sums of smooth strongly convex functions, one per agent, with communication restricted to neighbors in a graph. Existing decentralized algorithms typically emulate a {\it centralized} method; {\it the network serves only to exchange information}, from which agents approximate the global quantities that the method needs. It jointly determines how agreement is imposed, which variables are optimized jointly (blocks), and which connected subgraphs host the agents solving each block. GATE (Graph-Tearing message passing) instantiates the framework by assigning one dual variable per edge and partitioning the edges into trees. Agents interleave edge updates with local message passing recursions that summarize optimization within each tree (block). Its surrogate variant, GATE-S, uses tractable local models and compact messages to reduce computation and communication. We establish linear convergence and show that the topology-aware design acts as a \emph{preconditioner}: the rate depends {\it jointly} on topology and function geometry through the coupling between subproblems defined on the selected subgraphs, whereas consensus-based optimization methods pay the worst case of each separately, the centralized condition number times the inverse spectral gap. On tree-dominant graphs, convergence is provably faster: the rate scales with the tree {\it diameter}, linearly in the number of agents on rings and barbells against quadratically for non-accelerated consensus-optimization methods. Experiments support the predicted scaling and savings in iterations and communication.

papers.title: W-JEPA: Wavelet Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Wearable Activity Recognition
papers.summary: A major challenge in wearable device activity recognition is the heterogeneity across datasets in sensor placement, channel count, sampling rate and subjects. papers.title: Multi-Sensitive Distributional Fairness: Joint Wasserstein Audits and Shapley Allocation
papers.summary: Fairness audits with several sensitive attributes are often performed one coordinate at a time. This can miss purely intersectional disparities: a score may be independent of each sensitive coordinate while depending on their joint profile. Conditional expectations of this quantile process induce a monotone information game: every reveal order yields an exact martingale decomposition of the same joint disparity, while Shapley values provide an order-free attribution across sensitive attributes. Under independent sensitive attributes, the game reduces to a Hoeffding-ANOVA decomposition and Shapley splits each interaction energy equally among its members; under dependence, orthogonality is lost and explicit formulas reveal suppression and redundancy effects that marginal audits can hide. We give fixed-grid estimators and permutation calibration, and illustrate the framework on synthetic examples and ACSIncome. The resulting framework separates three questions that are often conflated: whether joint distributional parity holds, how a fixed joint disparity decomposes along an information path, and how that disparity can be attributed across sensitive coordinates without privileging an ordering.

papers.title: Learning in Strategic Queuing with Geometric Recharge: From Bandits to Systems
papers.summary: We study packet routing in queuing systems where queues act as selfish, myopic agents that use no-regret learning algorithms to select servers with unknown service rates. Equivalently, in terms of the total arrival and service rates, the condition $\sum_{i=1}^n λ_i < (1-λ_{\max})\sum_{j=1}^m μ_j$ is sufficient, and sometimes necessary, for stability under no-regret learning. papers.title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs

papers.title: Depth Memory
papers.summary: Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. papers.title: On the Monitorability of Natural Language Autoencoders: Identification vs Discrimination

Our rival accounts test only transcript-level truths, which the monitored language model's conversation settles, so these results bound the easiest case and leave claims about the monitored model's own processing untested. papers.title: Learning Source Structure: Bayesian Prediction with Transformers
papers.summary: A transformer trained on sequences whose source parameters are drawn afresh each time can learn only what the sequences share: the source family and its prior. papers.title: Texture Interpolation as Texton Matching
papers.summary: Texture interpolation asks what should lie between two textures. papers.title: Approximating Optimal Policies in Heterogeneous Asynchronous Multi-player Bandits
papers.summary: Motivated by applications to cognitive radio networks, multi-player multi-armed bandits (MMAB) have attracted considerable attention in recent years. papers.title: Recalibrating Many Questions with Few Labels: Minimax Rates and Identification Limits
papers.summary: Many related prediction problems, which we call questions, come with few labels each. What information can be shared across them, and what is actually necessary for good decisions? We answer both for recalibration, motivated by decision models such as Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) that return a probability for any yes/no question a developer writes. A predictor reports a probability $P$ with output law $μ$ on $m$ questions, each with $n$ labels and a nondecreasing map $g_j(p)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid P=p)$; the compound risk is the excess Brier score over the true maps, averaged over questions. Over maps within sup-distance $τ\le 1$ and total variation $V\le 2$ of one nondecreasing shape (fixed effects), the minimax compound risk is $(mn)^{-2/3}+\min\{τ^2,1/n\}+\min\{τ^2,V^2,(V/n)^{2/3}\}$ up to universal constants, for every non-atomic $μ$. A pooled isotonic fit with a per-question correction sized once, on held-out labels of all questions, attains it without knowing $τ$, $V$ or $μ$ ($n\ge 2$, $m\ge 3$); tuning each question on its own labels loses a factor of order $\min\{n,\log(m^2/n)\}$ when the maps differ by constants and $m^2/n$ is large. When the maps are drawn from an unknown prior (random effects), other questions need not identify the Bayes rule. The loss, the identification regret, is at most $2^{-n}$ once the law of a question's data is known, extending a bound of Skibinsky (1968) for coins, and in the worst case at least $β_\star^{-n}/(72\sqrt{n})$ at every finite $m$, where $β_\star\approx 3.583$. Beyond a few labels per question, what cannot be learned is nearly unnecessary. For constant maps (an uninformative predictor) and constant-map priors, the exponential base is exactly $β_\star$, not the 4 suggested by the moment range; for monotone maps it lies in $[2,β_\star]$.

papers.title: Graph Metanetworks for Transformer Based Language Models

papers.title: Kairos: Transactional Security Enforcement at the System Boundary for LLM Agents
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively. A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmarks and three agent models, Kairos outperforms existing defenses in the trade-off between attack success and utility. papers.title: Beyond Task Success: A Theory of Representation Reuse
papers.summary: A learned representation is useful beyond its source task only if later tasks can make use of what the encoder has already learned. For such a family, we define the task-relevant state as the coarsest deterministic state sufficient for all of its tasks. A larger task family can require a finer state, and losing a required distinction makes at least one future task unrecoverable on a target support containing that conflict. Exact reuse also depends on how the retained information is presented to the downstream rule. We separate this into structural accessibility, which concerns whether the required distinctions remain recoverable, and coordinate consistency, which concerns whether those distinctions can be interpreted by the same downstream rule across samples. Both failure modes appear separately in the experiments. Reuse improves as task-relevant distinctions become more accessible. Reversible sample-dependent coordinate changes can sharply reduce reuse even when the representation remains recoverable, and inverting the applicable coordinate change restores performance. The same accessibility-reuse ordering appears in prospectively specified CIFAR-100 experiments with both ResNet-18 and DenseNet-121. Finally, preserving a candidate state that contains the distinctions needed by the anticipated task family improves reuse on compatible held-out tasks, with the clearest benefit when target supervision is limited. Representation reuse is therefore relative to the tasks that follow source learning: a useful representation must retain the distinctions those tasks need and make them available in a form that a shared downstream rule can use.

papers.title: Operator Surrogates
papers.summary: This chapter provides a mathematical introduction to operator surrogates, which are finite-parametric maps approximating complex (typically nonlinear) operators between infinite-dimensional (function) spaces. A typical approach to constructing operator surrogates is the encoder-approximator-decoder paradigm, whereby infinite-dimensional inputs are mapped to a finite-dimensional latent space, processed, and then mapped back to the infinite-dimensional output space. Subsequently, we survey key surrogate architectures, contrasting spectral methods, based on polynomial chaos expansions and related technologies, with more recent neural network approaches. We further discuss architectures that do not rely on representation systems, such as Fourier Neural Operators and transformers. We elaborate on their relationship and how they relate to other neural network operator surrogates, particularly those obtained by so-called "algorithm-unrolling". Additionally, we provide an introduction to the theoretical analysis of approximation and generalization errors. We explain how underlying low-dimensional structures, provided for example by holomorphy, are essential to overcome the so-called "curse of dimensionality": this refers to the fact that the complexity of numerical algorithms tends to increase exponentially in the problem dimensionality. We present convergence rate bounds for holomorphic operators that depend on the number of trainable parameters and the regularity of the input and output data. Throughout, we prioritize intuition over detailed technical proofs and provide precise pointers to the literature for detailed arguments.

papers.title: Anytime-Valid Certification of Robustness Margins for Safe Control via E-Values
papers.summary: Robust control uses the error between a known model and the true system as a robustness margin. papers.summary: Reachability analysis and set-based estimation for nonlinear systems require set representations capable of capturing nonconvex geometry. Hybrid Zonotopes (HZs) have recently gained attention because they can encode a union of up to $2^n$ polytopic components. Recent work has further shown that several HZ operations can be made \textit{sharp}, meaning that relaxing the binary variables yields exactly the convex hull of the represented set. However, no known HZ construction provides a sharp union of two convex sets that adds only one binary generator and no further continuous generators or equality constraints to those of the operands. This limitation affects scalability in repeated union operations, ReLU neural-network reachability, and nonlinear propagation methods that cover graph sets by unions of simpler sets. This paper identifies a connection between the exact closed-form convex-hull operation for Constrained Convex Generators (CCGs) and the binary-generator structure underlying HZs. We propose Hybrid Cones that can encode up to $2^n$ norm-cone components. Hybrid Cones inherit the logical structure of HZs while allowing richer convex components, including polytopic and norm-based sets. They support sharp unions requiring only one added binary variable and can represent unions and intersections of polytopes and ellipsoids. As a key application, we derive an exact representation of the ReLU graph using only two continuous and one binary generators. Numerical experiments for a localization problem with a nonlinear energy measurement function approximated by a neural network and the stability verification of the closed loop of a double integrator corrupted by a nonlinear disturbance with a saturated Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) controller show substantial reduction in representation size and reduced conservatism in comparison with HZs.

papers.title: Lipschitz Bounds for Neural Networks Using a Two-Copy Linear Fractional Transformation
papers.summary: This paper proposes a new method to bound the global Lipschitz constant of a neural network (NN). Our formulation uses a two-copy linear fractional transformation (LFT) representation of the NN with stacked signals. We use biased quadratic constraints (QCs) to bound the input/output behavior of the nonlinear activation functions. We then formulate a linear matrix inequality condition, using these biased QCs, to bound the Lipschitz constant of the NN. The best (smallest) Lipschitz bound is computed via a convex, semidefinite program. There are two key distinctions of the proposed two-copy formulation in comparison to existing methods that rely on a single incremental representation with incremental signals. First, the NN bias terms are eliminated in the standard incremental representation, but appear in our formulation. Second, there is a larger class of QCs that can be expressed for the nonlinearities in our formulation than in the incremental representation. We show that our proposed formulation yields less conservative Lipschitz bounds due to these two differences. We illustrate these points via several simple, motivating examples. We also demonstrate the proposed method using a benchmark problem with a NN controller for an inverted pendulum.

papers.title: DC-TORQ: Fast Assessment of Data Center-Induced Generator Torsional Oscillation Risk Quantification
papers.summary: The periodic power demand of large data centers can introduce forced oscillations into the power system. When these oscillations contain frequency components near a turbine-generator torsional mode, they may excite sustained shaft torque oscillations with amplitudes exceeding the allowable cyclic torque limits. Characterizing the impact of data center power oscillations on generator shaft torque requires accounting for frequency-dependent network coupling among the data center, the transmission network, and the generators. Although electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations can capture these interactions in detail, repeated simulations across excitation frequencies and load locations can be computationally demanding. This paper proposes an analytical framework for data center induced torsional oscillations that retains the coupled electrical and shaft dynamics. A detailed generator-network model is established, and closed-form transfer functions that map data center power perturbations to the torque in each shaft section are derived. Admissible shaft torque amplitudes are then translated into frequency-dependent limits on data center power oscillations. The proposed framework enables fast assessment of the shaft torque response while accounting for network dynamics and provides a quantitative screening criterion for candidate data center connection buses. The framework is validated on the IEEE benchmark model and applied to the IEEE 39-bus system.

papers.title: A Deficiency-Based Approach for Unbalanced Three-Phase Distribution System Expansion Planning
papers.summary: Distribution planners typically characterize grid needs through power flow studies and fit upgrades to those needs by hand. papers.title: Defense Filters for Robust Learning of Partially Observed Dynamical Systems
papers.summary: Robust estimation of unknown system dynamics from partial observations under attack is a core challenge in learning for control, increasingly critical in multi-agent networks subject to adversarial data poisoning. papers.title: NOCE-Net: Representation Learning for Battery Operational Context via Nested Sequence Modelling
papers.summary: Learning effective representations from battery operational history is essential for predictive health management and control-oriented applications. Existing approaches rely on response-dependent engineered features or short early-life windows, limiting generalisability and precluding use in prospective settings where future responses are unavailable. Our data pipeline, re-BatteryData, standardises heterogeneous aging datasets into semantically equivalent Full Equivalent Cycles (FECs) defined by absolute charge throughput, enabling end-to-end learning across diverse operational regimes. NOCE-Net combines multi-patch transformer encoders for intra-cycle dynamics with a GRU backbone for inter-cycle state evolution, operating on approximately $700$ batteries across ten public datasets spanning over $300$ operational profiles. In zero-shot evaluation on unseen battery chemistries and usage patterns, NOCE-Net achieves $13.7\%$ MAPE in voltage response prediction, outperforming strong long-sequence baselines by over $43\%$ while using $40 \times$ fewer parameters. Shape and component diagnostics of the learned hidden states reveal that the GRU's principal direction of evolution achieves Spearman $|ρ| \geq 0.95$ with the capacity fade trajectory on average across all datasets with monotone degradation profiles, including zero-shot test batteries, providing evidence that the representations encode degradation dynamics transferable to downstream tasks beyond battery response modelling. papers.title: Integer-Free Control Synthesis for Signal Temporal Logic via Ranked Implicants
papers.summary: This paper proposes an integer-free method for control synthesis of nonlinear discrete-time systems under finite-horizon Signal Temporal Logic (STL) constraints. Instead of introducing integer variables, we consider the discrete choices of the specification in a ranked order and solve a standard nonlinear program for each selected choice until a satisfying trajectory is found. We first define implicants as sets of timed atomic constraints whose joint satisfaction is sufficient to satisfy the specification. A reference trajectory obtained from a smooth approximation of the STL robustness is used to rank these implicants. Fixing one implicant turns the problem into a standard nonlinear program with no auxiliary weights or bilinear terms. If the solution does not satisfy the specification, the next implicant will be considered. We prove soundness and completeness of our method relative to the nonlinear programming solver. Numerical evaluation on nonlinear multi-agent systems shows that our proposed method identifies satisfying trajectories where the exact continuous reformulation fails, and moreover, it is faster than a mixed-integer formulation of the same specification.

papers.title: The Cost of Executability: Temporal Margins for Continuous-Time Multi-Agent Path Finding under Closed-Loop Control
papers.summary: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) solvers are evaluated on the schedules they produce, not on how well those schedules can be executed. Specifically, continuous-time optimal solvers can achieve even lower cost than their discrete counterparts by scheduling agents with near-zero temporal/spatial separation, and by exploiting graphs with higher connectedness; however, such schedules may prove hard to execute under a realistic controller. We integrate AOC-CBS, an anytime-optimal continuous-time MAPF solver, into a fleet coordination framework in which each agent tracks its timed path using model predictive control, and we evaluate the resulting system on congested MovingAI benchmark instances with 21 to 40 agents. Without intervention, only a fraction of the instances complete execution. We then apply T-robustness by adding a time-margin, i.e., a minimum temporal gap between agents at shared locations, as well as spatial inflation of the agent footprint. Increasing either margin raises execution success, for a relatively small increase in the schedule's sum-of-costs; it also improves how closely agents adhere to the schedule: when tracking each agent's position throughout execution and comparing it against the position it should occupy according to the schedule, the mean discrepancy falls significantly as the margin increases. In general, the two margins have different effects; temporal margin decreases deviation, giving the controller room to stay on schedule. Spatial margin affects deviation less and instead increases the clearance between agents, so that the same deviation no longer leads to a blocking stall. They are nonetheless substitutes rather than complements: spatial inflation is almost free in schedule cost, but its effect on execution success is small and does not compound with a temporal margin already in place.

papers.title: Traffic State Prediction and Control Using a Koopman Operator Framework with Polynomial Observables
papers.summary: In this paper, we develop a Koopman operator framework for modeling and control of traffic flow governed by the Lighthill--Whitham--Richards (LWR) conservation law. In contrast, the linearized LWR predictor is computationally cheaper but exhibits substantially larger prediction errors and yields a more conservative metering policy. These results demonstrate that the analytical structure of the nonlinear traffic conservation law can be exploited to construct an interpretable data-driven surrogate for efficient traffic prediction and control

papers.title: A Decoupled Approach for Modeling N-k Interdiction with Induced Failures in Electric Power Grids
papers.summary: The electric power grid is a critical infrastructure system subject to different types of failures which can have devastating impacts on society. One framework to study the resilience of the grid is the N-k interdiction model, which introduces an attacker and defender model to identify grid vulnerabilities. However, traditional N-k interdiction models characterize the power grid with steady-state assumptions. One key aspect missing from this analysis is the behavior of the grid as it evolves from the pre-failure grid state and post-failure grid state. During such a transition period, automated protection systems, transient instabilities, and other phenomena can trigger cascading failures that can occur before grid operators can respond. To bridge this gap, this paper first introduces the generalized induced failure N-k (N-k.k') problem, where an initial set of k failures induces an additional set of k' failures. In this context, we propose a disjoint optimization approach that decouples the computation of cascading failures from the interdiction model. This system response model, furthermore, is treated as a black box module without compromising the underlying performance guarantees of the interdiction model. Extensive experiments on several benchmark power grid case studies showcase the efficacy and scalability of the approach.

papers.title: Controllability of polynomial systems is undecidable and not recursively enumerable
papers.summary: Sontag conjectured in 1988 that global controllability of polynomial control systems with rational coefficients is undecidable, but that the controllable systems form a recursively enumerable set. We prove the first part of the conjecture and disprove the second. For every homogeneous polynomial vector field $F$ of odd degree with rational coefficients, we construct an explicit polynomial control system $Σ_F$, with one more state than $F$, that is globally controllable if and only if the origin is \emph{not} globally asymptotically stable for $\dot x=F(x)$. By a recent result, the homogeneous polynomial vector fields with a globally asymptotically stable origin form a set that is recursively enumerable but not decidable. Consequently, global controllability of polynomial systems is undecidable, and the controllable polynomial systems are not recursively enumerable. The same conclusions hold for systems of the form $\dotξ=f(ξ)+Bu$ with a polynomial drift and a constant input matrix.

papers.title: Braess' Paradoxes in Coupled Power and Transportation Systems
papers.summary: Transportation electrification introduces strong coupling between the power and transportation systems. In this paper, we generalize the classical notion of Braess' paradox to coupled power and transportation systems, and examine how the cross-system coupling induces new types of Braess' paradoxes. To this end, we model the power and transportation networks as graphs, coupled with charging points connecting to nodes in both graphs. The power system operation is characterized by the economic dispatch optimization, while the transportation system user equilibrium models travelers' route and charging choices. By analyzing simple coupled systems, we demonstrate that capacity expansion in either the transportation or the power system can deteriorate the performance of both systems, and uncover the fundamental mechanisms for such new Braess' paradoxes to occur. We also provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the occurrence of Braess' paradoxes in general coupled systems, leading to managerial insights for infrastructure planners. For general networks, by characterizing generalized user equilibria of coupled systems, we develop charging-pricing policies to mitigate Braess' paradoxes.

papers.title: Decentralized Stability Certificates for Interoperability in Power-Electronics-Dominated Power Systems
papers.summary: The rapid integration of power electronics converters has fundamentally altered the power grid's dynamic landscape, making modularity of operation and interoperability of heterogeneous devices two critical hurdles for power system reliability. In control language, these challenges can be paraphrased as decentralized certificates on the input/output behavior of every device, assured by local control, so that stability and guaranteed performance of the interconnected system emerge. For the power system application, such certificates should eventually be part of the rule book, the so-called grid code, and thus be generic and minimally restrictive for the control architecture of each device. Classical system-theoretic angles of attack to these questions go back to dissipativity concepts, which have historically been co-developed in automatic control, circuit theory, and power systems. Since standard dissipativity (e.g., passivity or small gain) criteria fall short in terms of conservatism, a range of more flexible and advanced tools have been developed to assure less conservative decentralized certificates guaranteeing stability under interconnection as well as dynamic performance following a disturbance. In this article, we review a range of methods that have been put forward to tackle these questions, compare and validate them, and point towards practically relevant research gaps which are amenable to control-theoretic approaches. Moreover, we provide a tutorial exposition of practically relevant power systems/electronics issues accessible to control engineers.

papers.title: Reduced Arc-Weight Heterogeneity for Master Stability Analysis of Directed Networks
papers.summary: Master stability analysis can be applied to directed networks even when their Laplacian matrices are not diagonalizable. Nevertheless, a diagonalizable Laplacian is easier to analyse because the perturbations governing synchronization separate into independent modes. This paper asks how many different positive coupling strengths are needed to obtain this simplification without adding or removing any directed connections. We first give an elementary construction showing that suitable positive weights exist for every weakly connected directed network and explain its relationship to stronger genericity results in the literature. We then introduce a measure of the smallest number of distinct coupling strengths required for diagonalizability. If a common coupling strength already produces a diagonalizable Laplacian, only one value is needed. For directed acyclic networks, we give a constructive upper bound based on the length of the longest directed path from a source. This bound is exact for rooted outward directed trees. Consequently, an outward star requires only one coupling value, whereas a directed path requires a different value on every arc. These results reduce coupling heterogeneity while retaining the simpler modal form of master stability analysis. Diagonalizability is treated as an analytical convenience, not as a sufficient condition for synchronization.

papers.title: Repeated Binary Direct Collinear Impacts Under Incremental Contact Laws With Residual Indentation: A Hybrid Systems Formulation
papers.summary: Incremental contact laws specify the normal contact force through a differential relation, possibly carrying an internal state, driven by the indentation and its rate. In some, the force is extinguished at a nonzero indentation, whether by plastic deformation or by an elastic aftereffect, so that a residual deformation remains at separation. Such laws sit uneasily within rigid body dynamics, which admits no deformation. The tension is tolerable when the indentation is small relative to the bodies, so that it may be carried constitutively rather than geometrically. Even then, the contact law alone does not determine the interaction of the bodies. Because force and indentation no longer vanish together, conditions for the commencement and termination of contact must be supplied separately. So must the fate of the deformation and internal state at separation, neither of which the equations of motion contain. This article formulates the repeated direct collinear impact of two convex bodies under external forces as a hybrid dynamical system. The contact interface is modeled as a massless element carrying the contact law and its state, coupled to the bodies through relative velocity and an interaction force dictated by the contact state. Consequently, all switching and resets are confined to the interface, leaving the geometry and the equations of motion of the bodies unaltered. The principal analytical properties of the resulting formulations are established, among them passivity and completeness; the branching of solutions at the onset and termination of contact is also examined. The framework is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

In the context of general nonlinear networked control systems, a standard approach for guaranteeing stability is to construct a storage function, coupled with a single timer variable, to analyze the maximum allowable transmission interval (MATI) and maximum allowable transmission delay (MAD). In this paper, we propose a new approach that assigns each signal that is either \textit{in transit or most recently updated}, to an individual timer variable. This enables the individual characterization and compensation for the dynamics of each potential updating error. Subsequently, based on a novel construction of timer-coupled storage functions, the dynamics of these timer variables is designed and investigated, leading to less conservative conditions on the MATI and MAD than those by the standard approach while still ensuring closed-loop input-to-state stability with respect to external disturbances. Finally, simulation results are given to illustrate the advantages of these new results.

papers.title: Rate-Cost Tradeoffs in Nonlinear Control
papers.summary: We study finite-horizon rate-cost tradeoffs for general stochastic control systems, including nonlinear systems. Under an average control cost constraint, we show that the minimum expected communication rate lies within an additive logarithmic gap above the normalized directed information minimized over causal control policies. This establishes directed information as the operationally relevant quantity governing rate-limited control, extending its previously established roles in causal source coding and linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control to general nonlinear control systems.

papers.title: Global stability of Michaelis-Menten networks
papers.summary: In a very nice paper, Blanchini, Breda, Giordano and Liessi studied networks of species coupled through Michaelis-Menten interactions. Under standard assumptions of strong connectedness and non-degeneracy, they show that there is a unique equilibrium, which is (locally) asymptotically stable. This note shows that global stability, which was stated there as an open problem, holds as well. In fact, whenever a positive equilibrium exists, it attracts every solution with positive initial condition, with no connectedness or non-degeneracy hypothesis at all; those assumptions are needed only in order to guarantee existence and to cover solutions starting on the boundary of the orthant. The key is to note that the system is contractive with respect to the Thompson part metric.

papers.title: Lifting Safety Through Reduced-Order Model Architectures: An Invariant Manifold Approach
papers.summary: Reduced-order model architectures are often used to decompose complex safety-critical control design tasks into tractable subproblems. In this paradigm, one must ask: when does the safety of a reduced-order model lift to safety of the full system? Taking an invariant manifold perspective, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of smooth, regular lifts of compact safe sets from reduced-order models. Our characterization relies only on asymptotic stability of an embedding of a reduced-order safe set, without additional robustness or rate conditions. We apply these results to study control barrier functions in reduced-order model architectures and lifts of safe sets through cascades. Further, we use our conditions to obtain topological obstructions to the tracking of safe, kinematic reduced-order models for mechanical systems. We conclude by using these obstructions to inform safe hierarchical control design for an underactuated satellite on SE(3).

papers.title: A Control Co-Design Framework to Optimize Sustainability with Application to Microgrid-Driven Data Centers
papers.summary: This work studies the optimization of physical plant characteristics and controller parameters for sustainability. Environmental sustainability is strongly correlated with the development and operation of energy systems, with data centers as the preeminent modern example. Data centers, and the grid technologies that provide their power, consume nonnegligible amounts of global energy and pose a risk to increase greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and electronic waste. Addressing such issues requires improved plant design and control strategies, often approached through optimization-based methods. However, there are noticeable gaps regarding data center and microgrid design: (i) simultaneous optimization of plant and controller features is rarely explored, and (ii) sustainability criteria are not emphasized. This work addresses these gaps by establishing a generalized, sustainability-centric control co-design (CCD) framework for energy systems. Uniquely, the CCD framework defines and categorizes sustainability metrics into three lifecycle stages - manufacturing, operation, and disposal - supporting optimization and comparative analysis of the metrics for different design options. To exemplify its use, the CCD framework is applied to a microgrid-driven data center system, providing a family of sustainability metrics correlated to plant and controller parameters. The analysis enabled by the framework supports the determination of tradeoffs between different types of environmental sustainability metrics. The system designs identified by the proposed framework show substantial improvements to environmental sustainability categories as compared to designs identified through baseline procedures.

papers.title: When is cumulative dose response monotonic? Analysis of incoherent feedforward motifs
papers.summary: We study the monotonicity of the cumulative dose response (cDR) for a class of incoherent feedforward motifs (IFFM) systems with linear intermediate dynamics and nonlinear output dynamics. While the instantaneous dose response (DR) may be nonmonotone with respect to the input, the cDR can still be monotone. To analyze this phenomenon, we derive an integral representation of the sensitivity of cDR with respect to the input and establish general sufficient conditions for both monotonicity and nonmonotonicity. These results reduce the problem to verifying qualitative sign properties along system trajectories. The structural conditions identify eight canonical IFFM models, four of which are analyzed in detail within the proposed framework. In particular, IFFM1 and IFFM3 exhibit monotone cDR despite potentially nonmonotone DR, while IFFM2 is monotone already at the level of DR, which implies monotonicity of cDR. In contrast, IFFM4 exhibits nonmonotone cDR. Numerical simulations indicate that these properties persist beyond the structured initial conditions used in the analysis. Overall, our results provide a unified framework for understanding how system structure shapes monotonicity in cumulative input--output responses.

papers.title: A Koopman--Polynomial Chaos Framework for SMPC of Nonlinear Stochastic Processes
papers.summary: This paper develops a polynomial parametric Koopman operator (PPKO) framework for stochastic model predictive control (SMPC) of nonlinear systems with parametric uncertainty and time-varying stochastic disturbances. The Koopman operator is parameterized by polynomial chaos expansions (PCEs), enabling data-driven nonlinear dynamics to be integrated with PCE-based uncertainty propagation and control. We show that the polynomial parameterization introduces no irreducible approximation gap beyond PCE truncation. We then derive a condensed deterministic SMPC reformulation that handles both time-invariant parametric uncertainty and time-varying disturbances while retaining an online optimization dimension that depends only on the control horizon and input dimension, independent of the lifted-state and PCE dimensions. The resulting formulation yields convex programs with expectation and second-moment constraints that can be solved using standard optimization methods. Numerical studies on the Duffing oscillator and the electrothermal cooling system demonstrate the accuracy, scalability, and closed-loop performance of the proposed framework.

papers.title: Lyapunov Exponents in Power Systems: A Survey of Theory and Applications in Stability, Control, Forecasting, and Protection
papers.summary: Lyapunov exponents (LEs) are fundamental metrics from nonlinear dynamical systems theory that quantify the average exponential rate of divergence or convergence of nearby trajectories in phase space. Over the past three decades, LEs have emerged as powerful tools across a wide range of power system problems, including transient and voltage stability assessment, chaos detection and mitigation, short-term load and renewable energy forecasting, and fault diagnosis. This paper presents a comprehensive review of these applications, covering more than 165 publications spanning from the early demonstrations of chaos in simplified machine models (1990s) to the most recent data-driven and machine-learning-augmented approaches applied to inverter-based resource (IBR)-dominated grids (2024--2026). The review is organized into four principal application domains: (i) stability analysis and real-time monitoring, (ii) chaos characterization and control, (iii) forecasting and predictability analysis, and (iv) protection, fault diagnosis, and condition monitoring. For each domain, we trace the evolution of methods, compare model-based and data-driven LE estimation strategies, identify key benchmarks and validation gaps, and outline the most pressing open research problems.

papers.title: MIXSim: A multiclass first order traffic model with composition-dependent dynamics for mixed-autonomy urban networks
papers.summary: This paper presents a novel multiclass first order macroscopic traffic model for mixed-autonomy in signalized urban networks, called MIXSim. Human driven vehicles (HDVs) and Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) are represented as separate classes while origin-destination information is retained through commodity specific states. The local vehicle class composition and class specific driving behaviour characteristics determine the parameters of a composition-dependent triangular fundamental diagram. At signalized intersections, the composition of movement demand additionally determines the saturation flow rate, while the realized movement flow is constrained by demand, effective green time, and downstream receiving capacity. Numerical experiments investigate different CAV penetration levels and CAV time gaps, together with alternative signal control strategies. The numerical experiments illustrate how changes in CAV penetration and CAV time gap affect network performance under the tested conditions, and demonstrate the use of MIXSim for comparing signal control strategies across different mixed traffic regimes.

papers.title: Public Battery Field Data
papers.summary: Battery systems and algorithms are developed and evaluated primarily on laboratory cycling data, but fielded battery systems are subjected to duty cycles, temperatures, and measurement conditions that cannot be reproduced in a lab. Field data from batteries in service has begun to appear in public releases attached to individual papers, but each release has its own format, units, labels, and other gaps that make it difficult to compare against others. We present a curated collection of 35 public field-data releases from 27 research groups, covering applications that span passenger EVs, buses, light electric mobility, grid-scale storage, distributed storage, consumer electronics, industrial robotics and satellites. Where the releases are complete enough to measure, this heterogeneous collection contains 256 GB of data from at least 149,188 lithium-ion cells, 3,187 batteries, 115.6 MWh of energy storage capacity, and 3,040 unit-years of service. Critically, it also contains 6,465 labeled or reported faults, which provide greater visibility into what real battery performance and safety issues look like outside the lab. We release a public repository of metadata and code for each of the field datasets. For each dataset it provides a registry entry with sources, license and access links, checksums to confirm a download is complete, a metadata table, and code for how to load it. We also report where released datasets differ from their papers. We hope the collection can help serve researchers (human or otherwise) as a useful platform for improving battery field diagnostics, fault detection and health estimation. Better field evidence can also feed back to improve manufacturing quality, inform second-life screening and residual-value estimates, and broadly accelerate electrification.

papers.title: Exploiting the Flexibility of LLM Inference for Frequency Regulation Service
papers.summary: While the widespread deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly driven up power demands in computing clusters, the unique execution characteristics of LLM inference offer a novel opportunity to utilize these clusters as controllable loads. First, we model the problem as a hierarchical Markov decision process that includes request-to-replica dispatching and token-level resource allocation. Then, we introduce a reward redistribution network to address the temporal asynchrony between millisecond-level scheduling decisions and second-level frequency regulation signals. Furthermore, we develop an optimization framework based on a mean-field approximation to enable coordination among a large number of replicas under high request concurrency. Simulations using real-world data demonstrate that the proposed approach accurately tracks frequency regulation signals without compromising service-level objectives.

papers.title: Diversifying Moving Target Defense Against Adaptive Attacks Through Factorized Diffusion
papers.summary: Proactive defense offers a means to enhance power-system cybersecurity through controlled modifications of system configurations. One example is moving target defense (MTD), which uses distributed flexible AC transmission system (D-FACTS) devices to perturb transmission-line reactances against stealthy false data injection attacks. Existing MTD methods primarily rely on deterministic optimization, producing a single perturbation plan for each operating condition. However, repeated or highly correlated plans may expose predictable system configurations that attackers can learn and exploit. To address this limitation, this paper reformulates MTD as a conditional generative problem that produces diverse, secure, and physically feasible perturbation candidates. Learning such a distribution is challenging because MTD decisions jointly involve selecting branches, determining perturbation magnitudes, and coordinating adjustments across the network. To make this problem tractable, we factorize the decision distribution into three sequential conditional stages: branch selection, magnitude allocation, and continuous refinement. Graph-conditioned diffusion models are employed to capture the discrete and continuous decisions while accounting for network dependencies. Furthermore, a - objective is incorporated into diffusion training to favor candidates with desirable defense effectiveness and operational costs. Numerical studies on the IEEE 118- and 300-bus systems show that the proposed framework achieves AC feasibility comparable to that of optimization-based MTD baselines and higher - values, while reducing online computation time by an order of magnitude. The generated candidate pool remains effective under changing operating conditions and device availability, providing diverse high-value alternatives for flexible online cyber defense.

papers.title: ConQUESTA: Topology-Aware Post-Training Structural Pruning of Quantum Neural Networks
papers.summary: Deploying quantum neural networks (QNNs) on sparse hardware requires preserving task accuracy while reducing compiler-induced two-qubit gates, SWAPs, and depth. We present ConQUESTA (\underline{C}onstrained \underline{Qu}antum \underline{E}ntangler \underline{S}election with \underline{T}opology \underline{A}wareness), a post training pruning framework that combines task saliency with compiler cost, screens candidate entanglers, and searches complete pruning masks under an explicit accuracy constraint. Unlike one-shot ranking, each mask is transpiled as a whole across multiple coupling topologies. Across 4-, 6-, and 8-qubit QNNs and eight model seeds at 55% pruning, ConQUESTA achieves mean resource reductions of 61.6% on Breast Cancer, 72.0% on Digits01, and 82.2% on Iris, exceeding the strongest matched simple baseline by 3.5, 1.7, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Fixed-mask recovery raises feasibility from 16/24 to 22/24 runs. In a fixed-k=4 scaling study on a scaling probe of 4 to 12-qubits, the raw mask space grew from 495 to 12.1M while the evaluated masks increase only from 189 to 305. Resource-weight changes alter depth/routing priorities with at most a 0.44-point mean validation shift.

papers.title: Vector-field-guided constraint-following control for path following of uncertain mechanical systems
papers.summary: Achieving dynamics-level control is a critical yet challenging problem for accurate, high-speed geometric path-following of uncertain robotic systems. This paper proposes a vector-field-guided constraint-following control framework for geometric path following of uncertain mechanical systems. Applications to an underactuated aircraft system and a fully actuated manipulator system demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of the framework.

papers.title: Teleoperation Operational Design Domain based on Minimal Risk Maneuver Capability
papers.summary: This article discusses the concept of an Operational Design Domain (ODD) designed specifically for teleoperated road vehicles. For this purpose, the ODD concept designed for automated driving is adapted for teleoperation. papers.title: Residential Peak Load Reduction via Direct Load Control under Limited Information
papers.summary: Thermostatically controlled loads and electric vehicles offer flexibility to reduce power peaks in low-voltage distribution networks. This flexibility can be maximized if the devices are coordinated centrally, given some level of information about the controlled devices. In this paper, we propose novel optimization-based control schemes with prediction capabilities that utilize limited information from heat pumps, electric water heaters, and electric vehicles. The objective is to flatten the total load curve seen by the distribution transformer by restricting the times at which the available flexible loads are allowed to operate, subject to the flexibility constraints of the loads to preserve customers' comfort. The original scheme was tested in a real-world setup, considering both summer and winter days. The pilot results confirmed the technical feasibility but also informed the design of an improved version of the controller. Computer simulations using the adjusted controller show that, compared to the original formulation, the improved scheme achieves greater peak reductions in summer. Additionally, comparisons were made with an ideal controller, which assumes perfect knowledge of the inflexible load profile, the models of the controlled devices, the hot water and space heating demand, and future electric vehicle charging sessions. The proposed scheme with limited information achieves 43.3 % and 27.8 % of the potential average daily peak reduction that the ideal controller with perfect knowledge would achieve in summer and winter, respectively.

papers.title: Prospect Theoretic Approach to Pursuit-evasion Differential Games with Risk Aversion and Probability Sensitivity
papers.summary: This paper considers pursuit-evasion (PE) differential games in which the pursuer's and evader's irrational perceptions of environmental uncertainty lead to deviations from rational controllers. Secondly, sufficient conditions for capturability are established in terms of irrationality parameters. Finally, the CPT-Nash equilibrium is analyzed by Brouwer's fixed-point and self-consistency theorem. The new results reveal that irrational behaviors benefit the pursuer in some cases and the evader in others. Certain captures that are unachievable under rational behaviors can be achieved under irrational ones. By bridging irrational behavior with game-based control, a theoretical foundation is established for human-machine control systems.

papers.title: Regularization in Data-driven Predictive Control: A Convex Relaxation Perspective
papers.summary: This paper explores the role of regularization in data-driven predictive control (DDPC) through the lens of convex relaxation. Using a bi-level optimization framework, we model system identification as an inner problem and predictive control as an outer problem. Within this framework, we show that several regularized DDPC formulations, including l1-norm penalties, projection-based regularizers, and a newly introduced causality-based regularizer, can be viewed as convex relaxations of their respective bi-level problems. This perspective clarifies the conceptual links between direct and indirect data-driven control and highlights how regularization implicitly enforces system identification. We further propose an optimality-based variant, A-DDPC, which approximately solves the inner problem with all identification constraints via an iterative algorithm. Numerical experiments demonstrate that A-DDPC outperforms existing regularized DDPC by reducing both bias and variance errors. These results indicate that further benefits may be obtained by applying system identification techniques to pre-process the trajectory library in nonlinear settings. Overall, our analysis contributes to a unified convex relaxation view of regularization in DDPC and sheds light on its strong empirical performance beyond linear time-invariant systems.

papers.title: Converter-Aware Coordination of Computing Flexibility in Behind-the-Meter Data Centers
papers.summary: Data centers are emerging as large electricity consumers whose demand can be reshaped through workload scheduling. However, computing flexibility in behind-the-meter facilities does not automatically translate into electrically realizable power flexibility. First, a task-level mixed-integer linear formulation preserves synchronous training configurations and completion requirements, while Minkowski-sum aggregation and Shapley--Folkman convexification yield a linear inference-pool representation without unit-level binary variables. The latter admits a conditional relative relaxation-gap bound that decreases inversely with pool size. Second, a four-node electrical model links computing demand, on-site injections, and grid exchange to converter and network limits through lifted voltage variables and second-order cone relaxation. Finally, a mixed-integer model coordinates workloads, photovoltaic generation, energy storage, and grid purchases. Case studies show that electrical limits reshape scheduling and renewable utilization, while on-site resources reduce grid dependence. Under the studied conditions, fixed training cannot support full inference service within voltage limits, whereas coordinated scheduling achieves negligible inference shortage and passes verification against the original alternating-current model. These findings demonstrate the role of computing--electrical coordination in realizing the operational value of workload flexibility.

papers.title: Modeling and Analysis of Dynamic Coupling Effects in a Free-Floating Space Manipulator
papers.summary: Motion of a robotic manipulator mounted on a free-floating spacecraft induces base translation and rotation, creating a dynamic coupling that affects end-effector motion. Singular value decomposition is then used to examine coupling strength, directional anisotropy, and the orientation of the coupled motions. Numerical maps show that coupling strength is invariant to the first joint angle but depends strongly on the relative configuration of the remaining joints. Increasing the spacecraft base mass reduces joint-to-base and end-effector-to-base coupling, while its effect on the joint-to-end-effector mapping is smaller and more dependent on configuration. The translational end-effector-to-base mapping is highly anisotropic in some configurations: its base-velocity ellipse becomes increasingly flattened as the weak coupling mode approaches zero. The principal end-effector and base velocity directions also change their relative alignment across the configuration space, producing predominantly opposing responses in some regions and transverse or approximately codirectional responses in others. Together, these results provide a geometric description of how coupling magnitude and direction vary with manipulator configuration and spacecraft mass.

papers.title: Optimization via a Control-Centric Framework
papers.summary: Optimization plays a central role in intelligent systems and cyber-physical technologies, where speed and reliability of convergence directly impact performance. By pairing a Lyapunov function with a selectable decay law, we obtain continuous-time dynamics with guaranteed exponential, finite-time, fixed-time, or prescribed-time convergence. The convergence regime thus becomes a design input: choosing among these regimes changes only the decay law, not the algorithm or its analysis. Within this framework, we introduce three feedback realizations of increasing restrictiveness: the Hessian-gradient, Newton, and gradient dynamics. These constructions unify unconstrained optimization, extend to constrained problems via Lyapunov-consistent primal-dual dynamics, and broaden results for minimax and generalized Nash equilibrium seeking problems beyond exponential stability, the last two through centralized solvers. In total, the framework spans six problem classes and four convergence regimes, yielding a unified design recipe across twenty-four combinations, some of which, to the best of our knowledge, have no direct continuous-time counterpart in the prior literature.

An analogous operation $\G_{SP}\lrarg \G_{PQ}\equivd \G_{PQ}$ can be defined in relation to graphs $\G_{SP}, \G_{PQ},$ on edge sets $S\uplus P, P\uplus Q,$ respectively in terms of an overlapping subgraph $\G_P$ which gets deleted in the right side graph (see for instance the notion of $k-sum$ \cite{oxley}). For matroids we define the `linking' $\M_{SP}\lrarm \M_{PQ} \equivd (\M_{SP}\vee \M_{PQ})\times (S\uplus Q)$, denoting the contraction operation by '$\times$'. In each case, we examine how to minimize the size of the `overlap' set $P,$ without affecting the right side entity. In the case of vector spaces, there is a polynomial time algorithm for achieving the minimum, which we present. Similar ideas work for graphs and for matroids under appropriate conditions. Next we consider the problem of decomposition. Here, in the case of vector spaces, the problem is to decompose $\V_{SQ}$ as $\V_{SP}\lrarv \V_{PQ},$ with minimum size $P.$ We give a polynomial time algorithm for this purpose. In the case of graphs and matroids we give a solution to this problem under certain restrictions.

papers.title: Probe Sets for Nonlinear Kalman Filtering: Multi-Center Gains and Covariance Recalibration
papers.summary: Kalman filters (KFs) choose the gain as the product of the state-measurement cross-covariance and the inverse of the innovation covariance. papers.title: Dynamic Attack Surfaces: A Queue of Branching Processes
papers.summary: Modern attack surfaces are inherently dynamic. Vulnerabilities emerge over time and they remain exposed to exploit until defenders discover and patch them. Finally, we show that equal proportional AI amplification of offensive and defensive capabilities need not preserve security: accelerating both sides can shift the defensive bottleneck and move the system into an unbounded-risk regime.

papers.title: Optimal Decay Matrix Control Barrier Functions: Soundness and Completeness for Matrix Safety Constraints
papers.summary: Many safety requirements, such as keeping a manipulator away from kinematic singularities, a network connected, or a system observable, amount to keeping a state-dependent matrix positive definite. The MCBF constraint bounds how fast the safety margin, the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix, may decay. Yet a fixed decay rule is conservative, rejecting safe controls that drive the state quickly toward, but never across, the boundary of the safe set. Scalar optimal decay (SOD) addresses this issue by scaling the decay term by a scalar weight that is optimized together with the control. For scalar barrier functions, SOD then rejects a control at the boundary only if the control would decrease the margin. For MCBFs, however, SOD can reject controls that leave the margin unchanged, and near the safety boundary SOD accepts such controls only at a high cost. We introduce matrix optimal decay (MOD), which replaces the scalar weight with a matrix multiplier while keeping the semidefinite program convex. MOD is provably sound and complete, certifying at the boundary exactly the controls that do not decrease the margin. If some control can strictly increase the margin at every boundary point, the MOD-MCBF filtered controller is continuous and renders the safe set forward invariant. We also add an optional recovery condition that drives the system toward the safe set after a violation without affecting soundness or completeness. On a planar two-link arm avoiding singularities, MOD-MCBF certifies safe motions that both a fixed decay rule and SOD reject, and tracks an end-effector target more closely than SOD.

papers.title: Adaptive Handling of Deadline Misses via Stochastic MPC
papers.summary: Real-time control systems may experience sporadic computational overloads that cause controller executions to overrun their expected deadlines, affecting the timely update of control inputs. Such overruns are classically handled with static decisions, e.g., by either stopping and discarding the late execution at the deadline instant, or continuing it while skipping the next activations. This paper first demonstrates that such static policies can lead to suboptimal performance when the controlled system undergoes varying operating conditions, and thus proposes a control-driven hybrid overrun strategy that optimally adapts the deadline miss handling at runtime. We evaluate our proposal on linear benchmarks including a double integrator and an aircraft pitch system.

papers.title: Infrastructure-Aware Runtime Protection of Co-Deployed AI Services at the Industrial Edge
papers.summary: In modern production lines, a single edge device simultaneously runs multiple AI services like a torque-control model, a vision inspector, a predictive maintenance routine. All these services run on the same CPU and same shared network segment. When the shared network segment saturates, the services do not crash. The services just produce outputs that are inaccurate or stale, and no longer reflect the plant's conditions. Our paper targets this class of silent, partial failure scenarios in Industrial Edge Systems. We treat each co-deployed service as an autonomous agent. We introduce the Runtime Criticality Score (RCS), which each service agent uses to express at any moment, its intrinsic utility and survival urgency under resource constraints. The score is computed from six normalized dimensions covering physical consequence, inference quality, input freshness, recent availability stress, actuator coupling, and available protective actions on the host. Its dimension weights are adjusted online through a lightweight Bayesian update driven by the type of disturbance currently observed, so the same service is ranked differently under a network delay than under thermal throttling. Agents publish their RCS to peers over an open, peer-to-peer discovery channel, and use it to negotiate three things without a central controller: (i) local threshold enforcement on their own host, (ii) migration to a willing peer when the current host can no longer protect them, (iii) reassignment of the coordination role when the incumbent coordinator is itself impaired. Beyond the immediate benefit of catching silent degradation, the framework contributes a concrete instance of decentralized, physically grounded agent coordination. Agents belonging to different owners can advertise capabilities, bid for protection, and reorganize across an open network.

papers.title: On Over-Conservatism Under Low-Probability Extreme Events: A KL-Regularized Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Planning Method
papers.summary: The increasing penetration of renewable energy makes power systems more vulnerable to low-probability extreme events, elevating system planning to a critical role in ensuring reliability. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) based on the Wasserstein distance is widely used to address this challenge. However, we find that the conventional Wasserstein ambiguity set tends to excessively amplify the probabilities of low-probability extreme events, leading to over-conservative investment decisions. To mitigate this over-conservatism, this paper proposes a novel ambiguity set that modifies the Wasserstein distance with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization term. By leveraging the KL divergence's sensitivity to relative probability changes, the proposed set effectively curbs the unrealistic magnification of low-probability events. A two-stage distributionally robust planning model built upon this new ambiguity set is developed to optimize the installed capacity of photovoltaic, wind, and energy storage. The complex model is then reformulated as an equivalent exponential cone program with strict theoretical proofs, making it computationally tractable. Numerical results on the PJM 5-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems reveal the over-conservatism of standard Wasserstein DRO under low-probability extreme events and validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed planning model and solution algorithm.

papers.title: Fast Analytical Method for Resource Adequacy Assessment in Renewable-Rich Power Systems

papers.title: Generic Local Identifiability Does Not Imply Generic Global Identifiability in Linear Networks
papers.summary: We give a counterexample to the implication from generic local to generic global identifiability for linear networks with a fixed topology, independently unknown edge coefficients, and selected excited and measured nodes. A six-node network with nine unknown coefficients has exactly two compatible parameter vectors generically. Adding six excited and measured nodes preserves this ambiguity while making the added coefficients directly recoverable. The resulting twelve-node structure has forty-two independent unknown coefficients and zero diagonal. For every positive bound on the largest eigenvalue magnitude, a nonempty open set of parameters has two distinct compatible networks satisfying that bound. This holds for both real and complex coefficients. Other open regions have exactly one admissible solution. The proof uses a rational transformation exchanging the two solutions and a common limiting matrix whose fourth power vanishes. Exact rational-number certificates verify an explicit pair. The construction also extends algebraically when the unknown coordinates are whole rational transfer functions. Genericity in prescribed numerator and denominator coefficient families, and the requirement that every transfer function vanish at infinite frequency, remain separate questions.

papers.title: Beyond Planning: Differentiable Control-in-the-loop End-to-End Autonomous Driving

papers.title: Safe Driving in Occluded Environments
papers.summary: Ensuring safe autonomous driving in the presence of occlusions poses a significant challenge in its policy design. While existing model-driven control techniques based on set invariance can handle visible risks, occlusions create latent risks in which safety-critical states are not observable. Our key technical enabler is the application of probabilistic invariance: It relaxes the strict observability requirements imposed by set-invariance methods that demand the knowledge of risk-critical states. The proposed techniques provide linear action constraints that confine the latent risk probability within tolerance. Such constraints can be integrated into model predictive controllers or embedded in data-driven policies to mitigate latent risks. The proposed method is tested using the CARLA simulator and compared with a few existing techniques. The theoretical and empirical analysis jointly demonstrate that the proposed methods assure long-term safety in real-time control in occluded environments without being overly conservative and with transparency to exposed risks.

papers.title: Comprehensive Comparisons of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms in Autonomous Driving
papers.summary: This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of four representative reinforcement learning (RL) methods in autonomous vehicle (AV) decision-making, including: Fitted Value Iteration (FVI), Rollout Classification Policy Iteration (RCPI), Deep Q-Network (DQN), and a discrete-action adaptation of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (D-DDPG). papers.title: Robust Real-Time Monocular Human Pose Estimation with Insole-Based Sensor Fusion
papers.summary: Real-time monocular human pose estimation is an important sensing component for human-centered intelligent systems. While recent camera-based methods have achieved impressive accuracy, fundamental challenges persist, particularly when visual observations are incomplete, such as during lower-body occlusion or short out-of-frame intervals. In these challenging but common scenarios, vision-only systems often struggle to reconstruct physically plausible lower-limb motion and reliable foot-ground contact. Due to the highly unobtrusive and wearable nature of smart insoles, this paper investigates whether simple plantar pressure and acceleration sensors can effectively resolve these visually induced limitations. To systematically investigate this, we first collect a synchronized multimodal dataset and then propose a part-decoupled temporal fusion framework. The proposed model fuses foot-sensing features into the lower-body branch to compensate for incomplete visual evidence, while a lightweight coordinator exchanges information between the upper- and lower-body temporal representations to maintain whole-body consistency. The framework is evaluated with three representative real-time visual backbones based on 2D keypoints, 3D landmarks, and SMPL-based human mesh recovery. We evaluate our framework on three representative real-time visual backbones. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that incorporating simple foot sensors consistently improves pose accuracy, motion smoothness, and gait-related measurements over vision-only baselines, with the most significant gains observed under occlusion and short visual-dropout conditions. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that unobtrusive foot sensing provides vital and complementary physical observability when camera observations are temporarily unavailable.

papers.title: Learning Rewards in Strategic Games
papers.summary: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.

papers.title: EgoRayFormer: Ray-Space Stereo Refinement for Egocentric 3D Human Pose Estimation
papers.summary: Head-mounted stereo fisheye cameras provide a compact view of the wearer's body, but strong distortion, partial visibility and a short baseline make 3D pose estimation difficult. For each joint, the decoder projects shared 3D hypotheses along and around its viewing ray into both images. A geometric branch then corrects the projected joint locations and intersects the resulting rays; a learned gate blends this geometric estimate with a learned pose update. This formulation introduces an explicit stereo constraint while retaining flexibility when the rays provide weak depth constraints. In local evaluations on the official device-relative test splits, EgoRayFormer achieves three-seed mean MPJPEs of 17.64 mm on UnrealEgo2 and 49.55 mm on UnrealEgo-RW, improving to 47.57 mm with UnrealEgo2 pre-training. In paired validation ablations, removing the geometric branch increases MPJPE in all three seeds at both input resolutions. With a common ResNet-18 encoder and input resolution, our system reduces RW test MPJPE by 9.09 mm relative to the device-relative EgoPoseFormer baseline. papers.title: MMTA: Benchmarking Multimodal Temporal Analysis with Time Series, Text, and Vision
papers.summary: Time-series analysis is increasingly studied in multimodal settings, yet most benchmarks pair temporal signals with text or with visualizations derived from the same signal. papers.title: Accelerated Execution of Bayesian Neural Networks using a Single Probabilistic Forward Pass and Code Generation
papers.summary: Machine learning models perform well across domains such as diagnostics, weather forecasting, NLP, and autonomous driving, but their limited uncertainty handling restricts use in safety-critical settings. Traditional neural networks often fail to detect out-of-domain (OOD) data and may output confident yet incorrect predictions. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) address this by providing probabilistic estimates, but incur high computational cost because predictions require sampling weight distributions and multiple forward passes. The Probabilistic Forward Pass (PFP) offers a highly efficient approximation to Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI) by assuming Gaussian-distributed weights and activations, enabling fully analytic uncertainty propagation and replacing sampling with a single deterministic forward pass. We present an end-to-end pipeline for training, compiling, optimizing, and deploying PFP-based BNNs on embedded ARM CPUs. Using the TVM deep learning compiler, we implement a dedicated library of Gaussian-propagating operators for multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks, combined with manual and automated tuning strategies. Ablation studies show that PFP consistently outperforms SVI in computational efficiency, achieving speedups of up to 4200x for small mini-batches. PFP-BNNs match SVI-BNNs on Dirty-MNIST in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and OOD detection while greatly reducing compute cost. These results highlight the potential of combining Bayesian approximations with code generation to enable efficient BNN deployment on resource-constrained systems.
